situation: When Henry Ford was considering someone for a senior position, he often took the candidate out to lunch and ordered soup for them. He watched closely as the soup arrived. What was he looking for?
solution: He watched whether the candidate added salt to the soup before tasting it. Salting before tasting meant acting before gathering the facts, which showed a lack of judgment. For Ford, that was a red flag against hiring the person.
keyFacts: He watched whether they salted the soup before tasting it
Salting before tasting showed poor judgment, acting without the facts
hints: It isn't about table manners or how fast they eat.
Watch what the candidate does before the first spoonful.
Would you season something you haven't tasted yet?

title: The Roller Coaster Excuse
situation: Two boys come home very late from an amusement park. They tell their father: 'We were on the roller coaster, but as we went down the first hill the engine blew out!' Their father immediately grounds them for lying. How did he know?
solution: Once a roller coaster has gone over the first hill, it does not use an engine at all. It runs on gravity for the rest of the ride. An engine could not have blown out as they went down the first hill, so the father knew the story was made up.
keyFacts: Roller coasters don't use an engine after the first hill
The rest of the ride runs on gravity, so the story is impossible
hints: The lie is in the technical detail of their story.
Think about what makes a roller coaster move once it goes over the top.
After the first climb, nothing is pushing the cars except one natural force.

title: The Slowest Camel Wins
situation: A dying father tells his two sons they must race their camels to a distant city, and the one whose camel arrives last will inherit his fortune. For days the brothers wander slowly, each trying to hold back. Finally they ask a wise man for advice, and afterwards they race to the city as fast as they can. What did he tell them?
solution: The wise man told the brothers to swap camels. The fortune goes to the owner of the camel that arrives last, so each brother now wants the camel he is riding, which belongs to his brother, to get there first. Both race as fast as they can.
keyFacts: The wise man told them to swap camels
The prize goes to the owner of the last camel, not its rider
Each now rides his brother's camel and wants it to arrive first
hints: The rule is about whose camel arrives last, not who arrives last.
Nothing says each brother has to ride his own camel.
If you were on your brother's camel, how fast would you want it to go?

title: Half an Inch Too Tall
situation: A truck driver comes to an overpass and finds his truck is too tall to fit under it. He only needs half an inch. Rather than turn back or take the long way round, he gets a bright idea and drives through. What did he do?
solution: The driver let the air out of the trailer's air bags, its air suspension. With less air in them, the whole truck sat lower. That gave him the half inch he needed to get under the overpass.
keyFacts: He let air out of the trailer's air bags (suspension)
This lowered the truck enough to pass under
hints: He didn't change the bridge or the load. He changed the truck.
Part of the truck is held up by something he can let out.
Think about what would sink a little if you released some air.

title: Mary and Maria at the River
situation: Two sisters, Mary and Maria, had to cross a river. Mary walked across the bridge easily, but Maria jumped into the river and swam across. Afterwards, everyone said Maria was the smarter of the two. Why?
solution: The bridge was old and could only take the weight of a child. Mary was light enough to cross safely, but Maria was too heavy, so she wisely swam across instead of risking the bridge collapsing under her.
keyFacts: The bridge was old and could only take a child's weight
Maria was too heavy for the bridge, so swimming was the safe choice
hints: Mary's easy crossing doesn't mean the bridge was safe for everyone.
Consider the condition of the bridge and how old the sisters are.
What if one sister was much heavier than the other?

title: The Silent Signal at the Diner
situation: Two known robbers are followed by two plain-clothes police officers 24 hours a day. Every morning all four go to the same diner for breakfast. The robbers hang their hats and coats on the cloak-room rack, sit at opposite ends of the counter, eat in silence, put their things back on and leave. They never speak, never pass notes and make no obvious gestures, yet they pass detailed information to each other every day without the police noticing. How?
solution: The robbers use a code built from the cloak-room rack. The first robber picks particular hooks and hangs his clothes in particular ways. The second robber reads the pattern and replies by hanging his own things on other agreed hooks. The officers only see two men hanging up their coats, so they never notice the exchange.
keyFacts: The message is passed through the cloak-room rack
Which hooks they use, and how the hats and coats hang, is a pre-agreed code
The police see only ordinary coat-hanging and miss it
hints: The robbers do something every morning that looks completely ordinary.
Look closely at what happens before they sit down.
Which hooks they pick, and how they hang their coats and hats, carries the message.

title: Why $9.99?
situation: Today we are used to prices like $9.99 or $99.95 rather than neat round numbers like $10 or $100. The custom began in the late 19th and early 20th century, and at first it had nothing to do with making things look cheaper. Why were these odd prices first introduced?
solution: Odd prices were introduced to make the clerk open the cash register and give change on every sale. With a round price, a dishonest clerk could take a customer's whole-dollar note and pocket it without ringing up the sale. Because change was always needed, the clerk had to use the register, which recorded the sale and made a noise, and this deterred theft. The psychological effect on shoppers came later.
keyFacts: The point was to stop theft by clerks
An odd price means the customer needs change
Giving change forces the clerk to open the register, so the sale gets recorded
hints: The trick wasn't aimed at the customer at all.
Think about the person working behind the counter.
If the price is a round number, the clerk doesn't need to open the till to give change.

title: Not a Single Wet Hair
situation: Albert Amblefoot walked outside in a heavy rainstorm for half an hour. He wore no hat, carried no umbrella and held nothing over his head, and his clothes got soaking wet. Yet not a single hair on his head got wet. How could this happen?
solution: Albert is bald. He has no hair on his head, so no hair could get wet.
keyFacts: Albert is bald
He has no hair on his head to get wet
hints: The puzzle never says his head stayed dry.
Pay attention to exactly what stayed dry.
Think about how much hair Albert has.

title: Three Trucks Roll Over Him
situation: A man gets run over by three trucks. Most of the tyres on each truck roll right over him, yet they do not kill him. How is this possible?
solution: The man is down a manhole, underneath the manhole cover. The trucks' tyres roll over the cover above him, and he isn't hurt.
keyFacts: The man is down a manhole
The tyres pass over the manhole cover, not over his body
hints: The tyres never actually touch him.
Think about what could be between the man and the road.
He is below the road surface.

title: The Postman and the Dog
situation: A postman has to deliver a letter to a house surrounded by a five-foot wall. The only way to reach the house is along the main path, and a ferocious dog is tied by a long lead to a nearby tree, so the whole path is within its reach. If the postman walks up the path, the dog is sure to attack him. How does he outwit the dog and deliver the letter?
solution: The postman doesn't use the path at all. He throws the letter over the wall. The dog is tied to the tree and can't reach him there.
keyFacts: The postman avoids the path
He throws the letter over the wall
The dog is tied up and can't reach him at the wall
hints: Does the postman have to walk up to the front door?
The wall is only five feet high.
The letter can reach the house even if the postman doesn't.

title: Two Deaths and a Trip Home
situation: A girl killed two people. She never faced any consequences. The only thing that happened to her was that she got to go home. What is her name?
solution: Her name is Dorothy, from The Wizard of Oz. Her house landed on the Wicked Witch of the East and she melted the Wicked Witch of the West with water, and in the end she got to go home.
keyFacts: The girl is Dorothy
She is from The Wizard of Oz
hints: She isn't a real person.
It's a famous story in which the heroine just wants to go home.
Think of witches, ruby slippers and 'There's no place like home.'

title: Home by Eight
situation: A man phones his wife from work and tells her he won't be home until eight o'clock. He gets home at two minutes past eight, and his wife is furious with him. Why?
solution: He never said whether he meant 8 in the evening or 8 in the morning. He came home at 8:02 the next morning, after being out all night.
keyFacts: He didn't say AM or PM
He got home at 8 in the morning, not 8 in the evening
He had been away all night
hints: Two minutes late isn't the problem.
There are two eight o'clocks in every day.
Which eight o'clock did he actually get home at?

title: The Logic-Loving Cannibals
situation: While hiking in a remote jungle, you are caught by cannibals who love logic. They let you make one statement: if it is true, they will burn you, and if it is false, they will boil you in oil. What can you say to escape?
solution: You say: 'You will boil me in oil.' If that is true, they must burn you, which makes it false. If it is false, they must boil you in oil, which makes it true. The cannibals can't carry out either punishment without breaking their own rule, so they have to let you go.
keyFacts: You say 'You will boil me in oil'
The statement creates a paradox under their rules
Neither punishment can be carried out, so you go free
hints: The cannibals keep their own rules strictly.
Make a statement about what they will do to you.
Pick the statement that becomes false if they carry out the punishment it names.

title: The Dog That Stayed Dry
situation: A dog is on one side of a lake and its owner is on the other. The owner calls the dog, and it crosses the lake without getting wet. How?
solution: The water was frozen, so the dog simply walked across the ice.
keyFacts: The lake was frozen
The dog walked across on the ice
hints: The dog didn't go around the lake.
Think about the season.
Water isn't always liquid.

title: Who Wrote on the Wall?
situation: A student at school wrote something rude on the wall, and nobody owned up to it. Without a confession or a witness, the teacher still worked out who did it. How?
solution: The teacher had every student write a sentence on the board. One student's handwriting matched the writing on the wall, and that showed who had done it.
keyFacts: The teacher had every student write something
The culprit was found by matching handwriting
hints: The culprit gave himself away without meaning to.
Everyone was asked to do the same simple task.
Compare how each student writes.

title: Six Eggs, One Left
situation: There are six eggs in a basket. Six people each take one of the eggs. Yet one egg is still left in the basket. How can that be?
solution: The last person took the basket along with the last egg, which was still inside it. Everyone got one egg each, and there is still one egg in the basket.
keyFacts: The last person took the whole basket
The last egg was still inside the basket when it was taken
hints: Think about how each person took their egg.
Did everyone have to take their egg out of the basket?
One person took something more than just an egg.

title: Same Speed, Different Arrival
situation: Two cars drive from point A to point B. They travel at exactly the same speed along exactly the same route, so the trip takes each of them exactly the same time. Yet one car arrives about 34.73 minutes after the other. How is that possible?
solution: One car simply left point A 34.73 minutes earlier than the other. Both trips take the same time, but because they started at different times they also arrive at different times.
keyFacts: The cars did not leave at the same time
One car left 34.73 minutes earlier
hints: Nothing unusual happens on the road.
The puzzle tells you how long the trip takes, but not when it begins.
Ask yourself whether they both started at the same moment.

title: Regret at the 23rd Storey
situation: A woman jumps off a 33-storey building. As she falls past the 23rd storey, she immediately regrets her decision. What is going on?
solution: She is bungee jumping from the 24th storey of the 33-storey building. As she passes the 23rd storey, just after jumping, she gets scared and wishes she hadn't done it, but she is tied to a bungee cord and is safe.
keyFacts: She is bungee jumping
She jumped from the 24th storey, so she has only just jumped
She is attached to a cord and is not in danger
hints: She is not trying to hurt herself.
She did not jump from the roof: the 23rd storey comes right after she jumps.
She is tied to something stretchy.

title: Younger Five Years On
situation: Kiran was 20 years old in the year 1980. In the year 1985, he was only 15 years old. How come?
solution: The years are B.C. Kiran was born in 2000 B.C., so in 1980 B.C. he was 20 years old, and in 1985 B.C. he was 15. Before Christ, the year numbers count down as time moves forward, so 1985 B.C. came five years before 1980 B.C.
keyFacts: The years are B.C.
He was born in 2000 B.C.
B.C. year numbers get smaller as time passes, so 1985 B.C. came before 1980 B.C.
hints: Nothing is wrong with Kiran or with his records.
Kiran lived a very, very long time ago.
Think about which way the year numbers count before year 1.

title: Two Fathers, Two Sons, Two Apples
situation: There are two sons and two fathers. The first father gives two apples to his son, and the other father gives two apples to his son. Yet there are only two apples altogether. How can that be?
solution: There are only three people: a grandfather, a father and a son. The middle man is both a son (of the grandfather) and a father (of the boy), so two fathers and two sons are only three people. The grandfather gives two apples to his son, who hands the same two apples on to his own son.
keyFacts: There are only three people: grandfather, father and son
The middle man counts as both a father and a son
The same two apples are passed down
hints: Count the people, not the roles.
One person could be described in two ways.
Think of three generations of one family.

title: An Extraordinary Moment in 1978
situation: Something very extraordinary happened on the 6th of May, 1978, at 12:34 a.m. What was it?
solution: Nothing happened in the world itself; it was about the numbers. Written as a time and date, the moment was 12:34 on 5/6/78, and the digits run in order: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8.
keyFacts: It is about how the time and date are written
12:34 5/6/78 gives the digits 1 to 8 in order
hints: It isn't a historical event.
Write the time and the date down next to each other.
Write the date as month/day/year.

title: Robbed, Then Arrested
situation: Three men rob a house and get away with hundreds of thousands of euros. Yet it is the owner of the house who gets arrested. Why?
solution: The owner of the house was an accomplice of the robbers. He was in on the robbery, so it was the owner the police arrested.
keyFacts: The owner was an accomplice of the robbers
The robbery was an inside job
hints: The owner is not as innocent as he seems.
Did the owner know about the robbery beforehand?
The owner and the three men were working together.

title: The Sleepover Spider
situation: Five girls are at a sleepover. One of them yells, 'There's a spider on the wall!' and the others all scream, 'Kill it!' Yet the spider gets away alive. How?
solution: They all yelled for somebody to kill it, but nobody actually did. The girls were all too scared of the spider to go near it, so it escaped.
keyFacts: Nobody actually tried to kill the spider
The girls were too afraid of it
hints: Shouting 'kill it' is not the same as doing it.
Think about how the girls feel about spiders.
None of them was brave enough to go near it.

title: Five Litres in a Three-Litre Pot
situation: In a skills test, a teacher gives a student an open pot that can hold only 3 litres of water. He tells the student to bring 5 litres of water from the market. How can the student bring 5 litres of water in a pot that only holds 3 litres?
solution: He makes two trips. First he fills the pot to the brim and brings those 3 litres to the teacher. Then he goes back, fills the pot two-thirds full and brings the other 2 litres, making 5 litres in all.
keyFacts: He makes more than one trip
3 litres on the first trip and 2 litres on the second
hints: Nobody said it all had to come at once.
The market isn't going anywhere.
Add 3 and 2.

title: No Punch Thrown
situation: Two boxers are in the ring for a fight scheduled for 12 rounds. The fight is stopped in the 6th round, yet not a single punch has been thrown. How can this be?
solution: One of the boxers was a boxer dog, not a human fighter. That is why the fight could be stopped in the 6th round without any punches being thrown.
keyFacts: One of the 'boxers' was a boxer dog
The word 'boxer' is a pun on the dog breed
hints: Think about the other meaning of the word 'boxer'.
Not both fighters were human.
A boxer is also a breed of animal.

title: Joshua and the Three Deadly Doors
situation: Joshua is trapped in a room with three doors. The first door leads to acid gas that can melt a human body, the second to a room full of traps and unseen lasers that can cut a body, and the third to five robots programmed to kill humans. Which is the safest room?
solution: The safest room is the one Joshua is already in. Every door leads somewhere deadly, but nothing in the room where he is trapped is dangerous, so the best choice is to stay put.
keyFacts: The safest room is the one Joshua is already in
He doesn't have to go through any of the doors
hints: Look closely at what the question asks you to choose between.
Does Joshua have to open any of the doors?
One room is described as safe, and he is standing in it.

title: Four People in a Giant Box
situation: Dave, James, Carla and Anne are trapped in a giant box. It is completely dark inside, and they cannot see out. They shout for help until a man hears them and goes to the police station, telling the police that there are four people inside who cannot escape. The police then say the man who called for help is the one who set the trap. How do they know?
solution: The man who went for help was the one who built the giant box to trap Dave, James, Carla and Anne. Nobody could see into the dark, closed box, so the only way he could know exactly four people were inside was that he had put them there. He called the police himself to avoid suspicion, but what he knew gave him away.
keyFacts: Nobody could see inside the box
The man still knew exactly how many people were inside
He knew because he had made the trap himself
hints: Think about what the man told the police.
Could anyone outside the box actually see who was in it?
How would he know the exact number of people inside?

title: The Rooster's Egg
situation: A rooster lays an egg right on the peak of a triangular barn roof. Which way does the egg roll, left or right?
solution: It rolls neither way, because roosters do not lay eggs. Only hens lay eggs, so there is no egg to roll.
keyFacts: Roosters don't lay eggs
So there is no egg to roll
hints: Don't worry about the shape of the roof or the wind.
Think about the animal in the question.
Which chickens actually lay eggs?

title: Falling Without a Parachute
situation: You are falling through the sky without a parachute. There is nothing to grab and no one to help you. What do you do?
solution: You wake up, because you are dreaming. Falling with no parachute and no way out is a familiar nightmare, and it ends when you wake.
keyFacts: You are dreaming
The answer is to wake up
hints: This isn't about any survival trick.
Where do people most often find themselves falling like this?
You are probably lying in bed.

title: Leaving and Returning on a Friday
situation: A man travels to a city in another country on a Friday. He spends two days there. When he returns from that country, the day is Friday again. How is this possible?
solution: The page says his journey crosses the International Date Line. Crossing the line changes the calendar date, so the day he gets back can again be a Friday even though he spent two days away.
keyFacts: The trip crosses the International Date Line
Crossing the line changes the calendar day
hints: Think about where in the world he is travelling.
Time zones can do strange things to the calendar.
There is a line on the map where the date itself changes.

title: The Kind Beggar's Money
situation: A very kind beggar has 5 dollars. He finds another 5 dollars, then buys 3 biscuits at 1 dollar each. How much money does he have left?
solution: He has 2 dollars left. Because he is very kind, he gives back the 5 dollars he found instead of keeping it. He buys the biscuits with 3 of his own 5 dollars and keeps the other 2.
keyFacts: He returns the 5 dollars he found
He spends 3 of his own 5 dollars
He has 2 dollars left
hints: The simple sum, 7 dollars, is not the answer.
One word in the description of the beggar matters.
What would a very kind person do with money he found?

title: Two Women on the Balcony
situation: Two women on a balcony see two men walking towards them. One says to the other: 'Here come our fathers, the husbands of our mothers, the fathers of our children, and our own husbands.' How can this be true?
solution: The two women are married to the two men, who are also their fathers. Each woman married the other woman's father, so each man is one woman's father and the other woman's husband. Together the two men are the women's fathers, the husbands of their mothers, the fathers of their children and their own husbands.
keyFacts: Each woman is the daughter of one of the men
Each woman married the other woman's father
So together the two men fill every role she lists
hints: There are only two men, but each one plays more than one role.
Each man doesn't have to play every role for the same woman.
Picture two widowers, each marrying the other's daughter.

title: The Seven O'Clock Knock
situation: It is seven o'clock and you are asleep when there is a sudden knock on the door. Your parents are outside, and they have come for breakfast. What do you open first?
solution: You open your eyes first. You are asleep when the knock comes, so before you can open the door, the fridge or any food, you have to wake up and open your eyes.
keyFacts: You are asleep when they knock
The first thing you open is your eyes
hints: Forget about the breakfast food.
What state are you in when the knock comes?
Before you can open anything else, you have to wake up.

title: Eighty-Eight Hours in a Chair
situation: A man sat perfectly still in a chair for 88 hours. He never got up, never shifted and never moved at all. Why?
solution: He was dead. His body stayed in the chair for 88 hours before anyone found it.
keyFacts: The man was dead
His body stayed in the chair until it was found
hints: He wasn't meditating, and it wasn't a contest.
Nobody could sit that still for that long while alive.
What state was the man in?

title: Six Cups, One Move
situation: Six cups stand in a row. The first three are full of water and the last three are empty. By moving only one cup, you must make the row go full, empty, full, empty, full, empty. How do you do it?
solution: Pick up the second cup, which is full, and pour its water into the fifth cup, which is empty. Then put the now-empty second cup back where it was. Only one cup has moved, and the row now goes full, empty, full, empty, full, empty.
keyFacts: You pick up the second cup
You pour its water into the fifth cup
You put the empty cup back in its place, so only one cup was moved
hints: Moving a cup doesn't have to mean moving it to a new position.
What else can you do with a cup of water besides sliding it along?
Pour one of the full cups into one of the empty ones, then put it back.

title: The Horse and the Distant Hay
situation: A horse is tied to a rope 10 metres long. A pile of hay lies 11 metres away. The horse gets to the hay and eats it without breaking or stretching the rope. How?
solution: The other end of the rope isn't tied to anything. The horse has a rope around it, but nothing is holding it in place, so it can simply walk over to the hay.
keyFacts: The rope is only tied to the horse
The other end of the rope isn't fastened to anything
So the horse can walk freely to the hay
hints: Think about both ends of the rope.
The puzzle tells you what the horse is tied to, but not what the rope is tied to.
The other end of the rope isn't attached to anything.

title: Paying Rent with a Golden Chain
situation: A student has to pay his rent one day at a time, one gold link per day, for seven days. All he has is a golden chain of seven links, and he may make no more than two cuts in it. The landlord must have exactly as many links as days paid at the end of each day. How does he manage it?
solution: He cuts the chain into pieces of 1, 2 and 4 links. Each day he swaps pieces with the landlord so that the landlord always holds the right total. On day one he gives the 1-link piece. On day two he gives the 2-link piece and takes back the single link. On day three he gives the single link again. On day four he hands over the 4-link piece and takes back the others, and he carries on the same way until all seven links have been paid.
keyFacts: The chain is cut into pieces of 1, 2 and 4 links
The student and landlord swap pieces back and forth
Those pieces can make every total from 1 to 7
hints: The landlord doesn't have to keep every piece he gets.
You can give a bigger piece and take a smaller one back as change.
Pieces of 1, 2 and 4 links can add up to any number from 1 to 7.

title: Six Hens, Seven Boxes
situation: You have six hens and seven boxes. Every box must end up with something in it, and no box may be empty. How do you arrange them?
solution: Put one hen in each of six boxes. Then put one of those boxes, with its hen inside, into the seventh box. Now no box is empty.
keyFacts: One hen goes in each of six boxes
One of the boxes with a hen in it goes inside the seventh box
hints: Hens aren't the only thing that can go inside a box.
Could a box hold something other than a hen?
Put one hen-filled box inside the seventh box.

title: What Is a Greenhouse Made Of?
situation: A brown house is built from brown bricks. A white house is built from white bricks. What is a greenhouse made of?
solution: A greenhouse isn't made of green bricks. It's made of glass or another clear material that lets sunlight in to help the plants grow.
keyFacts: A greenhouse isn't made of green bricks
It's made of glass or another clear material that lets in sunlight
hints: Don't just follow the pattern.
A greenhouse is a building for growing plants.
What would let the most sunlight in?

title: The Pot That Never Fills
situation: A pot sits under a tap that is running all the time. The water keeps pouring in, yet the pot never fills up. Why?
solution: The pot has a hole in the bottom. The water drains out as fast as it comes in, so it never fills.
keyFacts: The pot has a hole in the bottom
The water leaks out as fast as it runs in
hints: The tap is working fine. Look at the pot.
The water goes into the pot, but it doesn't stay there.
Check the bottom of the pot.

title: The Road to Village A
situation: You come to a fork in the road. One road leads to Village A. A man is standing there who comes either from a village where everyone always tells the truth or from one where everyone always lies, and you can't tell which. You may ask him just one question. What do you ask to find the road to Village A?
solution: You ask: 'If I asked you which road leads to Village A, what would you say?' A truth-teller simply points to the right road. A liar would lie to the direct question, so he has to lie about that lie as well, and the double lie makes him point to the right road too. Whoever he is, you take the road he points to.
keyFacts: You ask him what he would say if you asked which road leads to Village A
A liar has to lie about his own lie, which cancels it out
Both kinds of man point to the correct road
hints: You don't need to know which village he comes from.
Find a question that gives the same answer whether he lies or tells the truth.
Ask him what he would say if you asked him which road goes to Village A.

title: One Poisoned Bottle in a Thousand
situation: A king has 1,000 bottles of wine, and exactly one of them is poisoned. The poison kills anyone who drinks it within 24 hours. He has ten prisoners to test the wine on and only one day to find the bad bottle. How can he be sure which bottle is poisoned?
solution: Number the bottles and write each number in binary. Ten binary digits are enough, because they can count past 1,000. Each prisoner stands for one digit, and he sips from every bottle that has a 1 in his position. After 24 hours, the prisoners who have died show where the 1s are. Read those digits as a binary number and you have the poisoned bottle.
keyFacts: Each bottle gets a number written in binary
Each prisoner stands for one binary digit and sips every bottle with a 1 in that place
The pattern of which prisoners die spells the poisoned bottle's number in binary
hints: Each prisoner can taste many bottles, not just one.
The pattern of who dies and who lives can carry information, like ones and zeros.
Write each bottle number in binary and give each prisoner one digit.

title: More Than Sixty Seconds
situation: How many seconds are there in a minute? If you answer 60, you are wrong. What is the answer?
solution: Now and then a leap second is added to Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) to keep clocks in step with the Earth's rotation. In the minute when that happens, there are 61 seconds, not 60.
keyFacts: Leap seconds are sometimes added to UTC
In those minutes there are 61 seconds
hints: Think about official timekeeping, not the clock on your wall.
Now and then, timekeepers change a minute on purpose.
Look up leap seconds.

title: Drowned on the Mountain
situation: A family of four went on a mountaineering holiday. On the second morning, all four were found dead in their cabin. There was no water damage in the cabin and no lake nearby, yet the coroner said they had all died from drowning. How is this possible?
solution: The family had climbed to a cabin high up the mountain, where the air is thin. Overnight they developed high-altitude pulmonary oedema, and their lungs filled with their own body fluid while they slept. They really did 'drown' from the inside, and no outside water was involved.
keyFacts: The cabin was at high altitude, where the air is thin
They suffered high-altitude pulmonary oedema
Their lungs filled with their own fluid, so they drowned without any outside water
hints: The water that killed them did not come from outside their bodies.
Think about what very high altitude does to the human body.
At high altitude, fluid can build up in the lungs while you sleep.

title: Shot Dead, No Investigation
situation: 'ONE MAN SHOT DEAD IN TRAGIC ACCIDENT.' This headline, and many like it, appeared in lots of newspapers last year. The death was mourned for a long time, yet there was no police investigation and no arrest. Why?
solution: The man was shot dead by accident while he was out hunting. It really was an accident and nobody did anything criminal. So the police had no reason to investigate or arrest anyone.
keyFacts: The shooting was a genuine accident
It happened during a hunting trip
There was no foul play, so there was nothing for the police to investigate
hints: Take the word 'accident' in the headline at face value.
Think of an ordinary activity where people carry guns legally.
He was shot by mistake while out hunting.

title: The Useless Expensive Equipment
situation: A man took an expensive piece of equipment with him on a journey. When he reached his destination, the equipment was in perfect working order, but it was of practically no use. Why not?
solution: The equipment was a piece of medical equipment. The place he arrived at had no patients and no medical needs. So although it worked perfectly, there was nobody to use it on.
keyFacts: The equipment was medical equipment
At the destination there were no patients or medical needs, so nobody needed it
hints: The equipment is fine. The problem is the place he took it to.
Think about who the equipment is meant to be used on.
It was medical equipment, and there was nobody there who needed treatment.

title: The Bomb That Won't Drop
situation: A pilot is flying a plane with a bomb on board. He presses the button and the door opens, but the bomb doesn't fall out. Why?
solution: The bomb is attached to the plane, or it is held inside the plane in a way that stops it from falling out. Opening the door does nothing if the bomb is not free to drop.
keyFacts: The bomb is fixed to the plane or held inside it
Because it is secured, it cannot fall even when the door is open
hints: The door opened properly. Nothing is wrong with the button.
Think about how the bomb is kept on board.
The bomb is fastened or held in place, so it can't drop through the open door.

title: Four Who Stayed at the Station
situation: A hundred people were waiting for a train at a station. When the announcer said the train had been cancelled, everyone left except four people. They had no medical problems, they could move and they had heard the announcement, yet they did not leave. Why?
solution: The four people were not waiting for the cancelled train. Either they were waiting for a different train that was still due to arrive, or they were station staff who had to stay at work whatever happened. The cancellation simply didn't affect them.
keyFacts: The cancellation did not affect those four people
They were waiting for a different train that was still coming, or they were staff who had to stay at the station
hints: Ask yourself whether all hundred people were there for the same reason.
Not everyone in a station is going on the same train, and some people aren't travelling at all.
They were waiting for another train, or they worked at the station.

title: Mr. Jones's Midnight Call
situation: In the middle of the night, while Mr. Jones was asleep in his hotel room, the telephone beside his bed rang. He woke up, picked up the phone and said 'Hello'. Then he put the phone down and went back to sleep. Who had telephoned him?
solution: Nobody had telephoned him. The call was the hotel's automatic wake-up service, which Mr. Jones had booked himself. No person was on the other end of the line.
keyFacts: No person called him
It was the hotel's automatic wake-up call
Mr. Jones had booked the wake-up call himself
hints: The question asks who called, but the caller may not be a person at all.
Hotels offer a service that rings your room at a set time.
It was an automatic wake-up call he had booked himself.

title: What Came Out of the Tap
situation: One night a woman found a spider in her bath. She screamed and got her son to flush it away. What came out of the tap the next day?
solution: A spider came out of the tap. It had been flushed away but survived, and it made its way back through the plumbing.
keyFacts: The spider survived being flushed
It came back out of the tap through the plumbing
hints: Being flushed away doesn't have to be the end of the story.
All the pipes in a house are connected in some way.
The spider survived and came back up through the pipes.

title: The Crying Man at Midnight
situation: At midnight, a man was walking alone down the middle of the street, crying. Later on he died. Why?
solution: While he was walking down the middle of the road at midnight, crying, a vehicle hit him and killed him. He was upset and not paying attention, and he was in the path of traffic.
keyFacts: He was walking in the middle of the road
A vehicle hit him and killed him
hints: Don't look for a hidden reason why he was crying. Look at where he was walking.
Think about what uses the middle of a street, even at midnight.
A car hit him.

title: The Lady and Her Dog
situation: A man is driving his car very fast, at about 80 km/h. Suddenly a beautiful lady with her dog crosses the street he is driving along. Does the car hit the lady or the dog?
solution: The car hits neither the lady nor the dog. The lady and her dog were never actually in the car's path, so there was nothing for it to hit.
keyFacts: The car hits neither of them
The lady and the dog were not in the car's path
hints: The question gives you two choices. Do you have to pick one?
Just because they crossed the street doesn't mean they were in front of the car.
Neither is hit, because they were never in the car's way.

title: Three Spies Under Questioning
situation: Three spies, Albert, Bertie and Cedric, are suspected of being double agents, and are questioned. Albert says: 'Bertie is a mole.' Bertie says: 'Cedric is a mole.' Cedric says: 'Bertie is lying.' Moles always lie and loyal agents always tell the truth. If there is only one mole, who is it? And if there are two moles, who are they?
solution: If there is only one mole, it is Bertie. Albert truthfully names him, Bertie lies about Cedric, and Cedric is right that Bertie is lying. If there are two moles, they are Albert and Cedric. Bertie is then telling the truth about Cedric, so Albert's accusation of Bertie is a lie, and so is Cedric's claim that Bertie is lying.
keyFacts: With one mole, the mole is Bertie
With two moles, the moles are Albert and Cedric
Cedric's statement directly contradicts Bertie's, so exactly one of those two is lying
hints: Start with the two statements that are about each other.
Cedric says Bertie is lying, so Bertie and Cedric cannot both be telling the truth, and they cannot both be lying either.
Test Bertie as a liar, then test Bertie as a truth-teller, and see what each case means for Albert.

title: The Two Children on the Porch
situation: A boy and a girl are sitting on the porch. 'I'm a boy,' says the child with black hair. 'I'm a girl,' says the child with red hair. At least one of them is lying. Which child is the boy and which is the girl?
solution: The child with black hair is the girl and the child with red hair is the boy. If only one of them were lying, both children would turn out to be the same sex, which is impossible because there is one boy and one girl. So both of them must be lying.
keyFacts: The black-haired child is the girl
The red-haired child is the boy
Both children are lying, because if only one lied they would both be the same sex
hints: What would happen if exactly one of them was lying?
If the black-haired child is telling the truth and the red-haired child is lying, you get two boys.
'At least one' turns out to mean both.

title: Shoes and Socks in the Dark
situation: You are in the dark. On the floor are six shoes in three colours and a heap of twenty-four socks, some black and some brown. How many socks and how many shoes must you carry into the light to be sure you have a matching pair of socks and a matching pair of shoes?
solution: You need 3 socks and 4 shoes. The socks come in only two colours, so among any three socks at least two must match. The shoes come in three colours, so three shoes could all be different, but a fourth shoe has to match one of them.
keyFacts: 3 socks
4 shoes
One more item than the number of colours guarantees a match
hints: You don't need to worry about how many socks there are in total.
Count the colours, not the items.
With two sock colours and three shoe colours, take one more than the number of colours of each.

title: Nine Dots, Four Lines
situation: Nine dots are arranged in a 3×3 grid. You must connect all nine using exactly four straight lines, without lifting your pencil from the paper. Every attempt inside the square seems to need five lines. How do you do it?
solution: You have to think outside the box, quite literally. The four lines must run past the edge of the 3×3 grid and turn outside it. Nothing in the rules says the lines have to stay inside the square formed by the dots.
keyFacts: The lines must extend beyond the boundary of the grid
The turns happen outside the square of dots
The idea that the lines must stay inside the square is a limit you set yourself
hints: Re-read the rules: what do they not say?
Who said the lines had to stop at the outer dots?
Let the lines run past the edge of the grid and turn out there.

title: What You Cannot See
situation: 'If you look, you can't see me. If you see me, you cannot see anything else. I can make you walk if you can't. Sometimes I speak the truth, and sometimes I lie. If I lie, I am nearer the truth.' What am I?
solution: The answer is darkness. When you look for it you see nothing, and when you are in it you can see nothing else.
keyFacts: The answer is darkness
Being in darkness means seeing nothing else
hints: Think about what happens when your eyes are open but see nothing.
It isn't an object or a person; it's a condition you can be in.
It arrives when the lights go out.

title: The Mystery Number Code
situation: Each four-digit number on the left turns into a single digit on the right: 9999 = 4, 8888 = 8, 1816 = 3, 1212 = 0. There is no arithmetic behind it. What is 1919?
solution: The rule is to count the closed loops in the way the digits are drawn. A 9 has one loop, an 8 has two, a 6 has one, and 1 and 2 have none. In 1919, each 9 gives one loop and the 1s give none, so the answer is 2.
keyFacts: The rule counts closed loops in the shapes of the digits
8 has two loops; 9 and 6 have one; 1 and 2 have none
hints: Stop doing sums and look at how the digits are drawn.
Why would 8888 score twice as much as 9999?
Count the enclosed holes in each digit.

title: Heads, Heads, Heads...
situation: I'm going to flip a coin four times. The first flip comes up heads. So do the second and the third. What are the odds that the fourth flip will come up tails?
solution: The odds are still 50%. Each coin flip is independent, so the three heads before it have no effect on the chance of tails on the fourth flip.
keyFacts: The chance is 50%
Each flip is independent of the previous ones
hints: Does the coin remember what it did before?
A streak feels meaningful, but does it change the coin?
Every flip starts from scratch.

title: Forests Without Trees
situation: 'I have forests, but no trees. I have lakes, but no water. I have roads, but no cars.' What am I?
solution: The answer is a map. A map shows forests, lakes and roads as symbols, but it contains no real trees, water or cars.
keyFacts: The answer is a map
The features are only pictured or symbolised, not real
hints: The forests, lakes and roads are all real features, but they aren't really there.
It's something you might use to plan a trip.
You can fold it up and put it in your glovebox.

title: Seven Eggs for Three Sons
situation: A man has three sons but wishes he had a daughter. God agrees to give him one, but only if he can first work out how to split seven eggs equally among his three sons. Seven does not divide by three, and he may not leave any egg out. How does he do it?
solution: He breaks every egg into the same container and mixes them until it is all liquid. Then he measures the liquid in millilitres and pours it into three equal parts. He could also scramble all seven eggs together and split the finished omelette into three equal portions by weight.
keyFacts: The eggs are broken and mixed together instead of being kept whole
The mixture is measured by volume or weight and split into three equal parts
hints: Nobody said the sons had to get whole eggs.
Think about what happens to eggs in a kitchen before they are eaten.
Crack them all into one bowl and measure what you get.

title: Ten Horses, Nine Stables
situation: A farmer has 10 horses in a field but only 9 stables. He still manages to get every horse into a stable. How?
solution: He puts one horse in each of the 9 stables. Then he puts the 10th horse into one of the stables with another horse, so two horses share a stable.
keyFacts: Nine horses go into the nine stables, one each
The tenth horse shares a stable with another horse
hints: Nobody said a stable can only hold one horse.
Think about sharing.
One stable ends up with two horses in it.

title: Teeth That Don't Bite
situation: I have teeth, but I don't bite. I am usually made of plastic, and you can carry me in your purse or pocket. You slide me through your hair. What am I?
solution: The answer is a comb. Its 'teeth' are the thin prongs that you pull through your hair when grooming it.
keyFacts: The answer is a comb
The 'teeth' are the prongs of the comb
hints: The teeth aren't in a mouth.
Think of something you use to get ready in the morning.
You use it to tidy your hair.

title: The Hole in the Donut
situation: Plenty of donuts are made without a hole, and they taste fine. Yet the traditional donut has a hole right through the middle. Why is it there?
solution: The hole lets the donut cook and fry evenly, so the dough is cooked all the way through instead of staying raw in the thick centre. It also makes the donut easier to coat and gives it its familiar look.
keyFacts: The hole makes the dough cook evenly all the way through when fried
Without it, the thick middle could stay undercooked
hints: Think about how donuts are cooked.
Which part of a thick lump of dough cooks last in hot oil?
Taking out the middle stops the centre from staying raw.

title: The Doctor's Six Patients
situation: You are a doctor at a top hospital with six gravely ill patients. Five urgently need organ transplants, but no organs are available. The sixth will die without a particular medicine, and if he dies, his organs could save the other five, because he is a registered donor. What do you do?
solution: You give Patient 6 the medicine and you do not take anyone's organs. Letting a patient die, or killing him, to use his organs is unethical and illegal, so the other five have to wait untreated until organs become available.
keyFacts: You give the sixth patient his medicine
You do not let him die or take his organs, because that would be unethical and illegal
hints: This isn't really a numbers puzzle.
Think about what a doctor is allowed to do for the patient in front of them.
His being a donor doesn't change what you owe him while he's alive.

title: Harried Hens
situation: A family kept a dozen egg-laying hens in their chicken coop. Late one night, a terrible storm hit the area and killed all but eight of the chickens. How many chickens does the family have now?
solution: The family still has twelve chickens. 'All but eight' died means eight survived, so four of the chickens are dead and eight are alive. The dead ones are still chickens.
keyFacts: The answer is still twelve chickens
Four are dead and eight are alive
'All but eight' means eight survived
hints: Read the wording of the question very carefully.
Does a chicken stop being a chicken when it dies?
Eight survived the storm. Count the ones that didn't as well.

title: Stolen Goods
situation: A woman in a department store fills her shopping cart to the top. Then she wheels it out of the store without paying. Nobody stops her, and she has done nothing wrong. Why not?
solution: The woman works at the department store. The cart is not full of merchandise: she has filled it with trash and is taking it out to the dumpster.
keyFacts: She is an employee of the store
The cart is full of trash, not goods
She is taking it out to the dumpster
hints: Nothing she takes out of the store is for sale.
Think about who she is and why she is in the store.
She works there, and the cart is full of something the store wants to get rid of.

title: Terrifying Tiger
situation: On a hot Saturday afternoon, a woman is walking slowly through the savannah when she spots a tiger in the distance. She doesn't turn around, hide or look for help. Instead she starts running towards the tiger. Why?
solution: The woman is visiting a zoo. The 'savannah' is part of the zoo, and the tiger is an exhibit, so she hurries over to see it and is in no danger.
keyFacts: She is at a zoo
The tiger is a zoo animal, so she is in no danger
hints: She is not afraid of the tiger at all.
She paid to be where she is on her Saturday afternoon.
The tiger is behind a fence and people come to look at it.

title: Tube Torment
situation: A woman enters a large metal tube. She is overcome with fear, clearly shaken, and grips her husband's hand tightly. He gently rubs her arms and speaks softly to her, but he is not bothered himself. A few hours later he tells her it is time to go, and her torment ends. What is going on?
solution: The metal tube is an airplane, and the woman is terrified of flying. She has to travel to see a dying relative, which makes her even more upset. Her husband comforts her as best he can during the few hours of the flight, and her ordeal ends when they land and get off.
keyFacts: The metal tube is an airplane
She is afraid of flying
Her torment ends when the flight lands and they get off
hints: The tube moves, and it carries many people.
Her fear is not about the tube itself but about where it goes, which is up.
She is on a plane and afraid of flying. The trip is to see a dying relative.

title: Smart Dad
situation: Jacob's dad couldn't stop his son playing video games: whenever he wasn't watching, Jacob went straight back to playing. So his dad fixed the problem for good with a hammer. Afterwards Jacob couldn't play any more, but his dad still could. What did he do?
solution: Jacob's dad used the hammer to put up a shelf high on the wall. He put the video game console and the controllers on the shelf, out of Jacob's reach. The dad could still reach them himself.
keyFacts: He used the hammer to put up a high shelf, not to smash the console
The console and controllers went on the shelf out of Jacob's reach
The dad is tall enough to reach them
hints: Nothing was broken.
The difference between Jacob and his dad is size.
The hammer was used to build something high up on the wall.

title: Locked Out
situation: After a long night of partying with her friends, a woman gets home and finds she can't get into the house. She is sure she is at the right home, and nothing is wrong with the door. Why can't she get inside?
solution: Earlier that night, as she started getting drunk, a concerned friend took her keys away so she wouldn't drive. The woman called and hired a driver to take her home. But she still didn't have her keys, so she couldn't unlock the doors.
keyFacts: She doesn't have her keys
A concerned friend took the keys because she was getting drunk
She got home with a hired driver, not by driving herself
hints: Something she normally carries is missing.
Someone took it from her for her own safety.
A friend confiscated her keys so she wouldn't drive drunk, and her house key was on the same ring.

title: Pile-up
situation: At the bottom of a large hill, more than 40 cars are involved in an accident. Some have overturned and others are resting on top of other cars. The pile-up is so big that a few military vehicles and a fire truck are also caught up in it. Yet nobody is hurt. How?
solution: The cars, trucks and other vehicles are toys. A small child is playing with them and has crashed them all together at the bottom of a hill.
keyFacts: The vehicles are toys
A small child is playing with them
hints: Nobody was in any of the vehicles.
The 'hill' might not be very big either.
Think of a child's playroom.

title: Sunny Day Weather?
situation: A man is driving on a sunny day. He makes a turn, and suddenly water pelts his car very hard for about five minutes. Then extremely strong blowing buffets the car until it shakes. The blowing stops, he turns back onto the main road and drives home safely. What happened?
solution: The man drove into a drive-through car wash. The water jets and then the powerful dryers hit the car. After about ten minutes he left and drove home in his clean car.
keyFacts: He drove into a car wash
The water and the blowing came from the car wash's jets and dryers
hints: The weather had nothing to do with it.
He chose to turn in there, and probably paid for it.
His car was a lot cleaner when he came out.

title: A Missing Man
situation: Three men enter a room, but only two walk out. Afterwards the room is empty. Where is the third man?
solution: The third man uses a wheelchair. He left the room with the other two, but he rolled out rather than walked out.
keyFacts: The third man uses a wheelchair
He left the room too, but didn't walk out
hints: All three men left the room.
Focus on exactly how each man left.
One of them can't walk.

title: The Bus Driver
situation: You are driving a bus, which is empty when you start your route. At the first stop four people get on. At the second stop eight get on and two get off, and at the third stop three get off and four get on. What colour are the bus driver's eyes?
solution: You are the bus driver, because the puzzle begins 'You are driving a bus'. So the bus driver's eyes are the same colour as your own. The passenger numbers are just there to distract you.
keyFacts: You are the bus driver
The answer is the colour of your own eyes
The passenger counts are a distraction
hints: You don't need any of the numbers.
Go back to the first sentence of the puzzle.
Who is driving the bus?

title: Five Men in the Rain
situation: Five men are travelling along a path, all at exactly the same speed, when it starts to rain. Four of the men walk faster and get drenched. The fifth man does not speed up at all, yet he stays completely dry. How can this be?
solution: It is a funeral. The four men who hurry and get soaked are the pallbearers. The fifth man stays dry because he is the dead man inside the coffin they are carrying.
keyFacts: It is a funeral procession
The four men are pallbearers carrying a coffin
The fifth man is the dead body inside the coffin
hints: The fifth man had no choice about how fast he moved.
The five men are not all travelling in the same way. Four of them are carrying something.
Think of a sad occasion where four men carry a heavy box on their shoulders.

title: Reginald Smyth's Vote
situation: Reginald Smyth, a 70-year-old man, was born in a small US town and never left it. One day he finds a note saying 'Meet me in the local cemetery at midnight.' He goes, hears a scream at midnight, and the next morning he is found dead beside a tombstone with his own name on it. An autopsy never finds out how he died. Who did Reginald vote for in the 1936 US presidential election?
solution: He voted for nobody. Reginald's small town was in Alaska, and Alaska did not become a state until 1959. As a resident of a territory rather than a state, he could not vote in the 1936 presidential election. The spooky details about the cemetery are there only to distract you.
keyFacts: He did not vote in the 1936 election
His town was in Alaska
Alaska only became a state in 1959, so he could not vote for president in 1936
hints: The cemetery, the scream and the tombstone have nothing to do with the question.
Think about where his small town was, and whether its people could vote for president in 1936.
In 1936 this place was a US territory. It did not become a state until 1959.

title: The Backwards Light Bulbs
situation: Railway trains and the New York City Subway have long used light bulbs that screw in backwards, the opposite way to ordinary bulbs. They give off just as much light as normal bulbs. Why go to the trouble?
solution: Bulbs with a reversed thread will not fit an ordinary home light fitting. That makes them useless to anyone who takes them home, so people stop stealing them from trains and subway stations.
keyFacts: People were stealing the bulbs
Reverse-threaded bulbs do not fit ordinary home fittings
So nobody has a reason to steal them
hints: The reason has to do with the people who use trains and stations, not with the electrics.
Ask yourself what might happen to ordinary bulbs left in a busy public place.
A bulb that won't screw into a lamp at home is not worth stealing.

title: The Knock at the Hotel Door
situation: A woman books a three-night stay at a singles hotel. On the second day, a man knocks on her door and says, 'Sorry, I thought this was my room.' She calls security at once. Why was she so suspicious?
solution: He knocked. If he really thought it was his own room, he would have used his key to get in, not knocked on the door. Knocking showed he knew the room belonged to someone else, so his excuse was a lie.
keyFacts: The man knocked on the door
Someone going into his own room would use his key rather than knock
So his excuse was false and he knew someone else was inside
hints: Think about what the man did, not what he said.
How do you normally get into your own hotel room?
Nobody knocks on the door of a room they think is their own. They use the key.

title: The Candle and the Tacks
situation: You have a book of matches, a box of tacks and a candle. You must fix the candle to a corkboard on the wall so that when it is lit, no wax drips onto the table below. How do you do it?
solution: Empty the box of tacks, then use the tacks to pin the empty box itself to the corkboard. Put the candle inside the box and light it with a match. The box works as a shelf that holds the candle and catches the wax. The page gives this as an example of 'functional fixedness': seeing the box only as a container for the tacks.
keyFacts: Empty the tack box
Pin the empty box to the corkboard with the tacks
Put the candle in the box and light it, so the box catches the drips
hints: Not everything you were given has to be used the way it normally is.
The box the tacks came in is more than just packaging.
Empty the box and fix it to the wall. It can become a little shelf.

title: The Round Manhole Covers
situation: Walk down almost any street and the manhole covers you step over are round rather than square, triangular or any other shape. This is not just tradition or looks: there is a practical reason for it. Why are manhole covers round?
solution: A round cover cannot fall through its own round opening, however you turn it. Almost any other shape, such as a triangle, square or pentagon, could be turned so that it drops into the hole. The page adds that a Reuleaux triangle, a special kind of rounded 'triangle', would not fall through either, and some covers of that shape do exist. Round covers also have other advantages: they are easy to make, they resist the pressure of the earth around them, they leave the most room for a person to climb in, and they can be rolled along.
keyFacts: A round cover cannot fall through its round opening in any orientation
Most other shapes, such as squares or triangles, could be turned so they drop into the hole
hints: Think about what could go wrong when a worker lifts the cover off and puts it back.
Imagine turning a square cover on its edge above a square hole.
A circle is the same width in every direction, so it can never slip down into its own opening.

title: A Square from Three Lines
situation: You are given three straight lines. Without breaking any of them and without adding any more, you must rearrange them to form a square. How do you do it?
solution: You arrange the three lines into the numeral 4. Four is a square, in the sense of a square number (2 × 2). The puzzle never said the square had to be the shape.
keyFacts: The lines are arranged to form the number 4
4 is a square number, so 'square' does not mean the shape
hints: Four sides are not possible with three lines, so think about what else 'square' can mean.
The answer comes from maths rather than geometry.
Which number can you write with three straight strokes, and what is it the square of?

title: A Cunning Mother-in-Law
situation: A mother-in-law hated her son-in-law so much that she wanted to poison him. But he was careful, and only ever ate what she herself ate. One night at dinner she cut a piece of meat in half, ate one half herself and gave him the other, and he died. How did she do it?
solution: She had smeared poison on only one side of the knife blade. When she cut the meat, only one half touched the poisoned side. She ate the clean half and gave him the poisoned one.
keyFacts: The poison was on the knife, not in the meat itself
Only one side of the blade was poisoned, so only one half of the meat was poisoned
hints: The meat was perfectly safe before it was cut.
Think about what touched the meat as it was divided.
A blade has two sides, and they don't have to be the same.

title: Trying Too Hard
situation: A salesman tries too hard to close a sale, and because of it he ends up dead. What happened?
solution: The salesman sold bulletproof vests. To prove to a customer how good they were, he put one on and insisted that the customer shoot him. The customer agreed but missed the vest and shot the salesman in the head.
keyFacts: He sold bulletproof vests
He wore one and asked the customer to shoot him as a demonstration
The customer's shot missed the vest and hit him in the head
hints: His demonstration was meant to show his product really worked.
The product was meant to protect the person wearing it.
He asked a customer to fire a gun at him, and the customer's aim was poor.

title: The Hunter's Fatal Shot
situation: A hunter aimed his gun carefully and fired. Seconds later he realized his mistake, and minutes later he was dead. Nobody shot back at him. What happened?
solution: He was hunting in snow-capped mountains. The noise of his shot set off an avalanche, which buried him. He suffocated under the snow.
keyFacts: He was hunting in snowy mountains
The gunshot set off an avalanche
He was buried by the snow and suffocated
hints: Where he was hunting matters a great deal.
The bullet didn't kill him, but the sound of the shot did.
Loud noises can be dangerous on snowy slopes.

title: A Fratricide
situation: A man kills his own brother in front of a crowd of people. Yet nobody reports him to the police. Why not?
solution: The man worked as an executioner, and his brother had been sentenced to death. Carrying out the execution in front of onlookers was his lawful job, so there was nothing to report.
keyFacts: The man was an executioner
His brother had been sentenced to death, so the killing was legal
hints: The killing was entirely legal.
The man was doing his job.
His brother had been condemned by a court.

title: Three Dead Men at a Card Table
situation: Three dead men are sitting at a table in a room. On the table are playing cards and a gun. What happened?
solution: The room was inside a submarine lying motionless on the sea floor, and the air was running out. The men had a gun with only two bullets, so they played cards for them. The two winners earned the right to shoot themselves, and the loser had to die slowly of suffocation beside the two corpses.
keyFacts: They were trapped in a submarine stuck on the sea bed and running out of air
The gun had only two bullets for three men
They played cards to decide who got a quick death; two shot themselves and the loser suffocated
hints: The men were trapped and knew they were going to die anyway.
Not all three died the same way, and the gun didn't hold enough for everyone.
They were in a submarine that couldn't surface, and they played for the bullets.

title: Colorblind
situation: A man died because he mixed up colours. How?
solution: In Thailand, when someone is bitten by a snake, the doctor has to identify the species to choose the right antidote. Tourists usually can't name the snake, so the doctor asks what colour it was and works out the species from that. The man was colourblind, gave the wrong colour, and received the wrong antidote.
keyFacts: He was bitten by a snake
The doctor chose the antidote based on the snake's colour as he described it
He was colourblind, so he described the wrong colour and got the wrong antidote
hints: He was a tourist abroad, in Thailand, and needed medical treatment urgently.
A doctor had to rely on his description of an animal.
He was bitten by a snake, and the antidote depends on the species.

title: Gone with the Wind
situation: If the wind hadn't blown so strongly that night, Angela would still be alive. What happened?
solution: Because it was windy, Angela went to a field to fly her kite. In the twilight she couldn't see the transmission tower nearby. Her kite got tangled in the power cables, and when she tried to free it she was electrocuted.
keyFacts: She went out to fly a kite because it was windy
The kite got tangled in power lines she couldn't see in the dusk
She was electrocuted trying to free it
hints: The wind didn't hurt her directly; it gave her a reason to go outside.
She was enjoying a hobby that needs wind.
Her kite got caught on something carrying electricity.

title: Deadly Scissors
situation: A woman is found dead in a hospital. The murder weapon was a pair of scissors. Yet her body has no cuts or wounds of any kind. How was she killed?
solution: The woman was in a critical condition, and the doctors had connected her to a machine that kept her alive. The murderer simply used the scissors to cut the machine's wires, and she died.
keyFacts: She was being kept alive by a life-support machine
The killer cut the machine's wires with the scissors
hints: The scissors never touched her.
Think about why she was in hospital and what was keeping her alive.
Something she was plugged into was cut.

title: Fire!
situation: Paul went scuba diving. He was later found burnt to a crisp. How could that happen?
solution: While Paul was scuba diving, a firefighting plane landed nearby to fill its tanks with water and sucked him in. He ran out of air while the plane was flying. The plane then dumped the water, with Paul in it, onto a burning forest.
keyFacts: A firefighting plane scooped up water where he was diving and sucked him in
He ran out of air while trapped in the plane's tank
He was dropped with the water onto a forest fire
hints: He was found far from where he went diving.
Something came down to the water and then flew away.
Firefighting aircraft refill their tanks from lakes and the sea.

title: The Birdwatcher
situation: An avid birdwatcher sees an unexpected bird. Soon afterwards he is dead. How come?
solution: He was a passenger on an aeroplane and saw a bird get sucked into one of the engines at 20,000 feet. The bird strike brought the plane down, killing him.
keyFacts: He was a passenger on a plane in flight
He saw a bird get sucked into the engine, which caused the plane to crash
hints: The bird was unexpected because of where he was when he saw it.
He was very high up at the time.
He was looking out of a plane window, near the engine.

title: A Premature Death
situation: A man knows he is going to die in a few days. But he dies even sooner than he expected. What happened?
solution: The man was seriously ill and had decided to donate his organs to a rich man. The rich man's son wanted to inherit his father's fortune. So he poisoned the donor, which meant the organs could no longer work in his father's body and the transplant could not save him.
keyFacts: The dying man was going to donate his organs to a rich man
The rich man's son poisoned the donor
The son did it to ruin the organs so his father would die and he would inherit
hints: The man's death was going to help someone else live.
Someone wanted that other person to die, not the man himself.
The man was an organ donor, and poison would make his organs useless to the rich man waiting for them.

title: Unsolved Crime
situation: Liz was just about to find out who killed Mario when she fell asleep. When she woke up, she realized she would never be able to find out. Why not?
solution: Liz was reading a novel on the beach, and Mario was the main character who had been killed. She fell asleep just before the murderer was revealed, with the book lying in the sand. When she woke up, the tide had come in and washed the book away.
keyFacts: Mario was a character in a novel Liz was reading
She fell asleep on the beach with the book in the sand
The tide came in and washed the book away
hints: Nobody in real life was killed.
Liz was somewhere relaxing, reading.
She was on a beach, and the sea took something from her while she slept.

title: What an Incredible Sight!
situation: A woman looks through a window and sees a man holding a knife. Yet she doesn't have enough time to call the police before she is murdered. Why not?
solution: The man wasn't outside at all. What she saw in the window was the reflection of the murderer, who was already inside her house, standing right behind her.
keyFacts: She saw a reflection in the window glass
The murderer was already inside the house, behind her
hints: The man was much closer than she thought.
Think about what a window shows you at night when the room is lit.
It was a reflection: he was standing right behind her.

title: Hang Up!
situation: A woman has just picked up her car from the mechanic. She dies because of a long telephone conversation. How?
solution: The mechanic had failed to fit the brakes on her car, and he tried to phone her to warn her. She was on another long call, so he couldn't get through. She never learned about the problem, and she died in a crash.
keyFacts: The mechanic hadn't fitted her brakes properly
He tried to call and warn her
Her line was busy because she was on another long call, so she crashed
hints: The phone call itself didn't hurt her. What mattered was the call she missed.
Someone badly needed to reach her.
The mechanic knew her brakes weren't working, but her line was busy.

title: There's Light
situation: Roger sees the light and freezes on the spot. Soon afterwards, he dies. What happened?
solution: Roger was a rabbit who had escaped from his home. While he was crossing a road at night, a car's headlights blinded him and he froze. The driver didn't see him and ran him over.
keyFacts: Roger was a rabbit
He froze in a car's headlights while crossing a road at night
The car hit and killed him
hints: Roger is not a human.
It happened on a road at night.
He was an animal caught in the headlights.

title: A Murderer
situation: Michael clapped his hands, and everyone in the room except him died. What happened?
solution: Michael was killing mosquitoes. The only other living things in the room were the mosquitoes, and he crushed them by clapping his hands together.
keyFacts: The ones who died were mosquitoes
He killed them by clapping them between his hands
hints: Nobody human died.
The victims were very small.
He was swatting insects between his hands.

title: Died of Fright
situation: A man woke up, lit a match, and saw something that frightened him to death. What did he see?
solution: The man was a prisoner who had planned an escape with the prison mortician. When the next inmate died, he would hide in that coffin, be buried outside the prison, and then be dug up by the mortician. He hid in a coffin and fell asleep, but the person who had died was the mortician himself. When he lit a match underground, he saw the mortician's body next to him and knew that nobody was coming to dig him out.
keyFacts: The man was a prisoner escaping by hiding in a coffin
The mortician was supposed to dig him up after the burial
The body in the coffin was the mortician, so no one would rescue him
hints: He woke up somewhere very dark and cramped.
He was trying to escape from somewhere, and he needed a partner outside.
He was buried in a coffin, and the corpse beside him was the man who was supposed to dig him up.

title: A Thief
situation: A man stole a wallet, and because of this he died. What happened?
solution: Inside the wallet was a card stating that its owner refused blood transfusions and organ transplants for religious reasons. The thief was later in an accident, and a blood transfusion would have saved his life. Because the doctors found the card and thought he was the wallet's owner, they didn't give him one.
keyFacts: The wallet held a card refusing blood transfusions for religious reasons
The thief was later badly hurt in an accident
Doctors took him for the owner and didn't give him the transfusion that would have saved him
hints: The owner of the wallet never hurt him.
Something written inside the wallet mattered after he was hurt.
Doctors thought he was the owner, who had refused blood transfusions.

title: Restless Sleep
situation: Paul comes home tired, goes to his room and turns off the light. Feeling uneasy, he keeps turning the light back on, looking around and turning it off again. After doing this several times, he looks under his bed and finds a dead body. What happened?
solution: A thief had been robbing Paul's home, and when Paul came back he hid under the bed. The strain was too much, and the thief had a sudden heart attack and died. Paul couldn't sleep because he kept hearing the ticking of the dead thief's wristwatch.
keyFacts: A thief hid under the bed when Paul came home
The thief died of a heart attack from the stress
The ticking of the thief's wristwatch kept Paul awake
hints: Paul didn't see anything when he turned the light on. Something else was bothering him.
The dead man was an intruder, and Paul didn't kill him.
Paul could hear a watch ticking under the bed.

title: An Open Door
situation: When Martin woke up that morning, he was surprised to see the door open. As soon as he stepped over the threshold, his head was bitten off. What happened?
solution: Martin was a canary who had lived in a cage for four months. His owner accidentally left the cage door open, and Martin flew out. Sylvester the cat had been waiting for exactly that chance, and caught and killed him.
keyFacts: Martin was a canary (a pet bird), not a person
The door was the door of his cage, left open by accident
A cat that had been waiting caught and killed him
hints: Martin is not human.
The door wasn't a door to a room or a house, and Martin had been kept behind it for months.
Martin was a small pet bird, and somebody else in the house had been watching his cage for a long time.

title: Death at the Wheel
situation: A woman is found dead in the front of a car. There is a gun on the back seat, out of her reach. The windows are closed and all the doors are locked. How did she die?
solution: The car was a convertible, and its top was down. The murderer shot her from outside and threw the gun onto the back seat. Nobody needed an open window or door to get at her.
keyFacts: The car was a convertible with the top down
The killer shot her from outside the car
The killer then threw the gun onto the back seat
hints: She did not shoot herself.
The killer never opened a door or a window.
Think about what kind of car doesn't need an open door or window for someone outside to reach in.

title: The Gift
situation: A dying man gives another man a gift, and then he dies. Shortly afterwards, the second man dies too. How come?
solution: The second man had shot the first man. Before he died, the first man handed him a grenade pin, which he had just pulled out of a grenade. The first man died, and then the grenade exploded and killed the second man.
keyFacts: The second man had shot the first man
The 'gift' was the pin from a grenade
The dying man had just pulled the pin, so the grenade then exploded and killed the second man
hints: The two men were not friends. The second man was the reason the first one was dying.
The gift was tiny and useless on its own. What matters is what it came from.
It's a small metal ring that the dying man had just pulled out of something explosive.

title: Death Under an Umbrella
situation: A couple find a man's body on the beach, lying under an umbrella with a knife on his back. There are no signs of violence and no blood anywhere. The autopsy shows that he died of natural causes. How can that be?
solution: The knife on his back was a tattoo. The man had simply died of a heart attack under his beach umbrella.
keyFacts: The knife was a tattoo on his back, not a real knife
He died of a heart attack (natural causes)
hints: The knife never hurt him.
The knife is 'on' his back, not 'in' it.
Beachgoers often show off body art. This knife was drawn into his skin.

title: A Lethal Dinner
situation: A woman is planning to kill her husband at dinner. But while she is making the meal, she kills herself instead. Why?
solution: She planned to poison her husband's food with pills she kept in her bag. When she reached for them, they were gone: her son had found them and eaten them, thinking they were sweets. She couldn't live with this tragedy and took her own life.
keyFacts: She planned to poison her husband with pills from her bag
The pills were missing because her son had eaten them, thinking they were sweets
Devastated by what had happened to her child, she killed herself
hints: Her plan was to poison him, and the poison was ready before she started cooking.
When she went to get the poison, it wasn't where she had left it.
Someone small in the house had found the pills and mistaken them for something tasty.

title: A Death in a Museum
situation: A man in a balaclava runs out of a museum with a painting under his arm. A police officer sees him and shoots him dead, then kills himself soon afterwards. A few days later, the man with the painting is buried and honoured as a beloved son of the city. What happened?
solution: There was a fire at the museum, and the museum's director went in to save the most valuable painting in the collection. The officer took him for a thief and ordered him to stop, but the director was deaf, didn't hear the warning and kept running, so the officer shot him. When the officer realised his terrible mistake, he took his own life. The director was honoured as a beloved member of the community at his funeral.
keyFacts: The museum was on fire and the man was the director, rescuing its most valuable painting
The officer mistook him for a thief and shouted at him to stop
The director was deaf, didn't hear the warning and kept running, so he was shot
The officer killed himself when he realised his mistake
hints: The man with the painting was not stealing anything.
Something dangerous was happening inside the museum, and he was saving the painting from it.
The officer did warn him before shooting, but the man couldn't hear the warning.

title: The Drinking Party
situation: Three drunk men and a dead body are found in a room. The men refuse to say anything to the police, yet the police quickly work out which of them is the killer. How?
solution: On the table was a bottle with a bloody mark from the dead man's head, so it was obviously the murder weapon. All four men's fingerprints were on it, because they had all been drinking from it. But only one man's fingerprints were upside down, which meant he had held the bottle by the neck like a club and struck the blow.
keyFacts: The murder weapon was a bottle they had all drunk from, with blood from the victim's head on it
