Every man's fingerprints were on the bottle
Only one man's prints were upside down, showing he had held it like a club to strike
hints: The murder weapon was something everyone at the party had handled.
Everyone's fingerprints were on it, so the police looked at how the prints were placed rather than whose they were.
You hold a bottle one way to pour a drink and the opposite way to hit someone with it.

title: Not Guilty?
situation: Igor breaks into Thomas's home to kill him, but he doesn't do it. Even so, he is arrested on the spot and convicted of the crime. Why?
solution: Igor was a hitman hired to kill Thomas. The person who hired him had also arranged for a second assassin to kill Thomas first, so that Igor would take the blame. When Igor arrived, Thomas was already dead and the police were there, so Igor was arrested and convicted of the murder.
keyFacts: Igor was a hired hitman
His employer had a second killer murder Thomas before Igor got there
Igor was caught at the scene with Thomas already dead and was convicted of a murder he didn't commit
hints: Thomas really was murdered, just not by Igor.
Igor wasn't acting for himself, and the person who hired him had another plan.
Someone else got there first, and the police were waiting when Igor arrived.

title: The Last Taxi
situation: Oscar was sitting reading his newspaper when he heard a noise. When he realised what had happened, he bitterly regretted not having caught the taxi in time. Shortly afterwards, he killed himself. Why?
solution: Oscar was a collector of model cars, and he was broke. He planned to sell his most valuable model, a taxi, to solve his money problems. After cleaning it, he didn't put it down securely on the table, and while he was reading it fell and smashed on the floor before he could catch it. With his last hope of money gone, he killed himself in despair.
keyFacts: The taxi was a valuable miniature model car, not a real taxi
Oscar was broke and was counting on selling it
It fell off the table and smashed before he could catch it, and he killed himself in despair
hints: 'Catching' the taxi doesn't mean getting a ride in it.
The taxi was very small and very valuable, and Oscar badly needed the money it would bring.
The noise was the sound of something falling off a table and breaking.

title: A Murder Outdoors
situation: A man walking down the street suddenly starts choking a woman who is walking past him. He is taken to the police station, but he is soon released. Why?
solution: The woman was his wife. Years earlier she had faked her own death, and he had been convicted of murdering her. According to the puzzle, because of double jeopardy he could not be prosecuted again for the same crime, so he was released.
keyFacts: The woman was his wife, who had faked her own death years before
He had already been convicted of her 'murder'
Double jeopardy meant he couldn't be tried again for the same crime, so he was released
hints: The man and the woman knew each other very well.
Everyone believed she had died years ago, and the man had already paid for it.
There is a legal rule that you cannot be tried twice for the same crime.

title: The Best Day of Her Life
situation: She thought it was the best day of her life, just moments before she died. What happened?
solution: At the end of a play, the lead actress came on stage and the audience began to applaud. At that moment the scenery failed and started to collapse onto the stage. The audience jumped up from their seats, screaming to warn her, but she thought it was a standing ovation. She stayed where she was and was crushed.
keyFacts: She was an actress on stage at the end of a play
The scenery began to collapse on her
She mistook the audience standing and screaming a warning for a standing ovation
hints: She was surrounded by a large crowd when it happened.
The crowd was on its feet and making a lot of noise, and she misread why.
She was an actress, and what she took for a standing ovation was a warning about the collapsing set.

title: A Blessing in Disguise
situation: A girl's mother died. At the funeral, the girl saw the man of her dreams and fell in love with him. Fourteen days later, she killed her sister. Why did she do it?
solution: She wanted to see the man again. She had only ever seen him at a funeral, so she reasoned that he might come to another family funeral. Killing her sister gave her one.
keyFacts: She wanted to see the man from the funeral again
She hoped he would come to another family funeral
Her sister's death would bring about that funeral
hints: The killing had nothing to do with anything her sister had done.
Think about the only place she had ever seen the man.
She needed another family funeral so that he might turn up again.

title: Shooting the King
situation: Alexander shot at the king, yet nobody condemned him for it. Why not?
solution: Alexander was playing poker and lost. In anger, he shot at the playing card showing the king.
keyFacts: The king was a playing card
He shot the card in anger after losing at poker
hints: No monarch was in any danger.
Alexander had just lost a game.
The king was printed on a playing card.

title: Start the Party!
situation: A man quits his job and celebrates by throwing a party that lasts all night. The next day he gets dressed up and jumps from the balcony of his house. Why?
solution: The man had won the lottery, so he resigned and celebrated with his friends. Days earlier he had accidentally destroyed the winning ticket by sending his suit, with the ticket in it, to the dry cleaner. He only found this out when he was getting ready to go and claim his prize, and he jumped from his balcony.
keyFacts: He had won the lottery and quit his job because of it
The winning ticket was destroyed when his suit was dry-cleaned
He found out while dressing to go and claim the prize
hints: He quit because he thought he no longer needed to work.
Getting dressed up the next day was part of an important errand, and something about his clothes mattered.
His winning lottery ticket had gone through the dry cleaning in his suit pocket.

title: The Terminal Taxi
situation: A taxi stops, the driver opens the door, and a dead man falls out onto the road. What happened?
solution: The previous passenger was a spider lover and had left a box with his spider in the taxi. When the dead man saw the spider he panicked, and the poisonous spider bit him.
keyFacts: An earlier passenger had left a spider in the taxi
The spider was poisonous
It bit the passenger when he panicked
hints: The driver had nothing to do with the death.
Someone who had ridden in the taxi earlier left something behind.
It was a box holding a poisonous spider.

title: The Creepy Game
situation: Jasmine was playing her usual favourite game when people suddenly started shooting at her. What happened?
solution: A hunting party on a frozen lake was using dynamite to blast an air hole in the ice. Jasmine, a dog, thought the dynamite was a stick and fetched it. The frightened men shot at her to make her drop it, but she hid under a jeep instead, and the dynamite exploded there.
keyFacts: Jasmine was a dog
Her game was fetching sticks, and she fetched a lit stick of dynamite
The men shot at her to make her drop it, but she hid under a jeep where it exploded
hints: Jasmine is not a person.
Her favourite game involves chasing and bringing back things that are thrown.
Hunters on a frozen lake threw dynamite to make a hole, and she brought it back to them.

title: The Quick-Witted Woman
situation: Thieves broke into a woman's house. She locked herself in her room and called the police, who told her no patrol cars were available and she would have to wait. Five minutes later, three patrol cars and an ambulance arrived at her house. What did she do?
solution: Two minutes after her first call, she rang the police again and said she had shot all the thieves. The police came straight away and caught the robbers. That is how she found out there were patrol cars available after all.
keyFacts: She called the police a second time
She falsely claimed she had shot the thieves
That made it an emergency needing an immediate response, including an ambulance
hints: She didn't deal with the thieves herself.
She made another phone call.
She told the police she had shot the burglars, which is why an ambulance came too.

title: A Well for Corpses
situation: Over many years, a man kills his sister, a friend, a girl he got pregnant and his boss, and throws each body into the same well. Every time, the body has vanished by the next day. Then he kills his mother and throws her in, and the next day her body is still there. Why?
solution: It was his mother who had been dragging the bodies out of the well all along. Once she was dead, there was nobody left to take her own body away.
keyFacts: His mother had been secretly removing the bodies from the well
She could not remove her own body
hints: The well itself is perfectly ordinary.
Someone had been cleaning up after him without telling him.
The person who took the bodies away was his last victim.

title: The Cave
situation: Lou is in a cave when he hears a strange sound outside. He goes out to see what it was and dies the moment he leaves the cave. What happened?
solution: The sound Lou heard was a chainsaw, used by a woodcutter who was felling a tree right in front of the cave. As Lou came out, the tree came down and he could not get out of the way. It fell on him and killed him.
keyFacts: The sound was a chainsaw
A woodcutter was felling a tree right outside the cave
The tree fell on Lou as he came out
hints: Nobody meant to hurt Lou.
The noise came from someone working just outside.
It was a chainsaw, and something big was about to come down.

title: Feather
situation: A man lies dead next to a feather. There is nothing else unusual about the scene. How did he die?
solution: The man was a sword swallower in a carnival side-show. While he was practising, with a sword down his throat, someone tickled his throat with the feather. He gagged, and the sword killed him.
keyFacts: He was a sword swallower
Someone tickled his throat with the feather while he was practising
He gagged with the sword in his throat and died
hints: The feather wasn't used to choke him or to poison him.
Think about what his job was. It was an unusual one, found at carnivals and side-shows.
He had a blade down his throat when someone tickled him with the feather.

title: Dry
situation: A man dies of thirst in his own home. He wasn't ill, and nobody locked him in. How could this happen?
solution: The man's home was a yacht, and he was sailing it around the world. Out on the ocean, he ran out of fresh water much faster than he expected, and he died of thirst on board.
keyFacts: His home was a yacht
He was out at sea, sailing around the world
His fresh water ran out sooner than he expected
hints: There was plenty of water all around him.
His home was not a house or a flat.
His home floated, and he was far out at sea when his drinking water ran out.

title: Sacred Death
situation: When the priest stopped talking, Bobby died. What happened?
solution: Bobby was a small hamster that his 9-year-old owner, Tom, had brought to church. During the sermon, the hamster escaped from the boy's lap and made its way to the altar area. When the priest finished speaking and walked back to his chair, he didn't see Bobby and crushed him with his foot.
keyFacts: Bobby was a hamster (a small pet)
He had escaped in church and ended up near the altar
The priest stepped on him by accident when he finished speaking and walked away
hints: Bobby is not a person.
Bobby was brought to church by a young boy and got loose during the sermon.
Once the sermon was over, the priest moved, and he didn't look where he was putting his feet.

title: The Daughter Disappeared
situation: Parents lose their young daughter at a playground, and eventually the police close the investigation. The parents take a medium to the park, who goes into a trance and tells them the girl is alive: her heart is beating, her lungs are breathing, she sees a luxurious house with expensive furniture, and there is only delicious food in her stomach. When they ask where their daughter is, the medium declares, 'She's all over the world!', and the parents collapse in tears. What did they understand?
solution: The girl had been kidnapped and sold for her organs. The medium's vision was of her organs, still working inside different people: a heart beating and lungs breathing in rich recipients' bodies in luxurious homes. Because the organs had gone to different people, she really was 'all over the world'.
keyFacts: The girl was kidnapped
She was sold for her organs
Her organs now live on in different recipients around the world
hints: The medium was describing parts of the girl, not the girl herself.
Why would a heart and lungs be in a luxurious house with rich owners?
She was abducted for a black-market trade in body parts.

title: A Car Without a Driver
situation: A car with nobody in it starts to move, and a man dies. No one was near the car at the time. How come?
solution: The murderer parked the car on a slope above the hot dog stand where the victim worked. He wedged a block of ice in the car to hold the brake pedal down, put the car in neutral, and then flew to another city so he wouldn't be suspected. It was a warm day, and when the ice melted the car rolled down the hill and hit the hot dog seller at his roadside stand, killing him.
keyFacts: It was a planned murder
A block of ice held the brake pedal down, with the car in neutral on a slope
The ice melted on a warm day and the car rolled down onto the victim's roadside stand
The killer had left for another city, giving himself an alibi
hints: It wasn't an accident, and the killer was nowhere near when it happened.
Something kept the brake pressed down for a while, then stopped doing so without anyone touching it.
Think of a timer made of something that melts on a warm day.

title: Shouldn't Have Looked Out of the Window
situation: A man looked out of a window and soon afterwards he died. What happened?
solution: The window he looked through was the window of his car, and he was driving. He saw a pretty woman, got distracted, and had a fatal accident.
keyFacts: It was a car window and he was driving
He was distracted by a pretty woman
He crashed and died
hints: He wasn't at home or in a building.
He was moving when he looked out.
He took his eyes off the road to look at someone attractive.

title: Punishment
situation: The killer was severely punished by his victim, and instantly. How?
solution: The 'victim' was a snowman. A man wanted to knock it down with his car and built up quite a lot of speed, but there was an iron pole sticking out of the ground in the middle of the snowman. He crashed into the pole.
keyFacts: The 'victim' was a snowman
The man tried to knock it down with his car at speed
There was an iron pole hidden inside the snowman, and he crashed into it
hints: The victim was never alive.
It was winter, and the 'killer' was behind the wheel.
Something solid was hidden inside what he was trying to smash.

title: Cry, Baby, Cry
situation: Cindy is in the middle of a crowd of people when she is murdered. Yet nobody notices her cries. How can that be?
solution: Cindy was watching a horror film in a cinema. During an intense, scary scene, while the whole audience was screaming, the murderer sitting behind her killed her. Her cries blended in with everyone else's screams.
keyFacts: She was in a cinema watching a horror film
Everyone was screaming at a scary scene
The killer sat behind her, and her cries blended in with the crowd's screams
hints: The people around her were making plenty of noise themselves.
The crowd was sitting in the dark, facing the same way.
They were all screaming, but at what was on the screen.

title: The Hanged Man
situation: John was walking across a snow-covered field when he came to a lonely tree with a man's body hanging from it. The man had died of strangulation the night before. Yet there were no tracks anywhere in the snow except John's own. How did the man get there?
solution: The hanged man was a skydiver. His parachute got tangled in the branches of the tree and the cords strangled him. He came down from the sky, so he left no tracks in the snow.
keyFacts: The man was a skydiver / parachutist
His parachute got caught in the tree and strangled him
He arrived from the air, so he left no tracks
hints: Think about ways to reach that tree without walking across the field.
He didn't come over the ground at all.
Look up: he came down from the sky, and something he was wearing got caught in the branches.

title: Sherlock Found the Killer
situation: Sherlock Holmes was walking down a corridor when he heard a woman scream, 'Please, John, don't kill me!' A shot rang out, and he burst into the room to find a dead woman and a gun in one corner, and a postman, a lawyer and an accountant standing in another. Holmes went straight to the postman and arrested him, and the postman really was the killer. How did Holmes know?
solution: The postman was the only man in the room. The lawyer and the accountant were both women. The victim had begged 'John' not to kill her, so the killer had to be a man, and only the postman fit.
keyFacts: The lawyer and the accountant were women
The postman was the only man
The victim called the killer 'John', a man's name
hints: Think about what the scream told Holmes about the killer.
The name 'John' matters. What does it tell you about the killer?
Don't assume the lawyer and the accountant were men.

title: The Dancing Dead
situation: A couple of dancers die during a dance competition. Nobody attacked them on the dance floor. What happened?
solution: It was a tango competition, and during their routine the couple passed a rose back and forth between them. A rival couple who badly wanted to win had poisoned the rose. The poison killed the dancers, and the rivals won the contest.
keyFacts: Their routine involved a rose they passed between them
A rival couple poisoned the rose
The rivals did it to win the competition
hints: Think about who would gain from their deaths.
Something they handled as part of their dance was deadly.
It was a tango, and a rose passed between the partners had been poisoned by rivals.

title: The Shooter
situation: Bill shot a man, and the man died. Yet Bill was not punished for it. Why not?
solution: The man was a film actor, and the script called for Bill to shoot him in a scene. By accident the gun had been loaded with real bullets instead of blanks. The shooting was a genuine accident, not murder, so Bill was not punished.
keyFacts: They were filming a scene where Bill was supposed to shoot the man
The gun was accidentally loaded with real bullets instead of blanks
It was an accident, so Bill was not to blame
hints: Bill was expected to pull the trigger.
Both men were working when it happened, and it was supposed to be make-believe.
It was a film scene, and the gun should have had blanks in it.

title: The Last Step
situation: Everybody knew that if Julia took one more step forward she would die, but nobody warned her. Why didn't anyone tell her?
solution: Julia was a rat that scientists were using in an experiment. She was trapped in a maze full of traps and was standing right in front of one. The people watching couldn't warn her, and they wouldn't have anyway, because the experiment was about seeing what she did.
keyFacts: Julia was a lab rat, not a person
She was in a maze full of traps set up by scientists
She was standing right in front of a trap
hints: Would Julia have understood a warning?
Julia isn't human.
She was an animal in a scientists' maze full of traps.

title: The Lady Killed the Lady
situation: Two white women are talking in the home of one of them, who lives alone. The guest goes into the bathroom, comes out five minutes later, and kills her host. Why?
solution: A Black friend of the guest had recently been killed, reportedly by the Ku Klux Klan. In the bathroom, the guest found a bloodstained KKK robe in her host's laundry hamper. The host was single, so the robe could only be hers. The guest took a nail file from the medicine cabinet, went out and killed her.
keyFacts: The guest's Black friend had recently been murdered, reportedly by the KKK
She found a bloodstained KKK robe in the host's laundry hamper
The host lived alone, so the robe was hers
She killed her with a nail file from the medicine cabinet
hints: The guest found something in the bathroom that changed everything.
It proved the host was involved in the recent killing of someone the guest loved.
A bloodstained Ku Klux Klan robe was in the laundry hamper, and her murdered friend was Black.

title: The Last Wine
situation: Camellia brought Valmont some wine. He looked at his watch, drank, and died. What happened?
solution: Camellia had offered Valmont a cruel game. She poisoned one of two glasses of wine, and he had to pick one to drink, and if he survived she would marry him. Valmont let the position of his watch's second hand decide which glass to take. He was unlucky and chose the poisoned one.
keyFacts: Only one of two glasses was poisoned, and he had to choose
If he survived, Camellia would marry him
He used his watch's second hand to pick at random, and picked the poisoned glass
hints: Valmont knew there was poison, and he drank anyway.
He had to choose between two glasses, and there was a prize if he chose right.
He used the second hand on his watch like a coin toss to pick a glass, and it picked the poisoned one.

title: Lucky Me
situation: Peter wins a raffle. Soon afterwards, he kills himself. Why?
solution: Peter was one of a group of people who were snowed in and running out of food. They held a raffle to decide which of them should die so that the others could eat the body and stay alive. Peter's name was drawn, so he had to take his own life.
keyFacts: Peter and others were trapped (snowed in) with no food
The raffle chose who would die so the others could eat the body
Being drawn meant Peter had to kill himself
hints: Winning this raffle was not good news.
Peter was stuck with other people somewhere they couldn't leave, and they had nothing left to eat.
The winner of the draw was going to become food for the rest of the group.

title: The Ship in the Ploughed Field
situation: A farmer ploughing his flat, dry field strikes something hard and uncovers the wooden hull of a large sailing ship, complete with cargo, buried in the soil. The field is far from any river and has not flooded in living memory, and nobody ever hauled the ship there. How did it get into his field?
solution: The ship sank centuries ago on the bottom of a shallow sea. Long afterwards, that part of the sea was closed off with dykes and pumped dry to make new farmland, so the old seabed, with the wreck still lying in it, became fields. The farmer is ploughing what used to be the sea floor, and the ship never moved at all: the water went away around it.
keyFacts: The ship sank normally, at sea, a long time ago
The land the field is on was reclaimed from the sea by draining it
The wreck never moved; the sea was removed from around it
hints: The ship reached that spot in the most ordinary way a ship can.
Ask not how the ship got to the field, but how the field got to the ship.
Think about countries that build dykes and pump water out to make new farmland.

title: Speeding on the Empty Road
situation: On a dead straight, flat and completely empty road in the far north, a lorry driver is pulled over and fined for doing 40 km/h. The officer tells him that at that speed he could have killed himself and the driver of the lorry approaching from the other direction, even though the two vehicles would never have touched each other or anything else. Why?
solution: The road is a winter ice road running across a frozen lake. A heavy lorry bends the ice slightly downwards as it goes, which pushes a pressure wave through the water underneath. If the lorry drives faster than that wave, or if its wave meets the wave of an oncoming lorry or bounces back from the shore, the waves pile up and can crack the ice open, so both lorries could have gone through into the freezing water. That is why ice roads have very low speed limits and strict rules about how close vehicles may pass each other.
keyFacts: The road runs over a frozen lake or sea
A heavy vehicle pushes a wave through the water beneath the ice
At speed, or when two waves meet, the wave can break the ice and the lorries would sink
hints: The danger is not a collision. Think about what is under the road.
The road only exists for a few months each year.
A heavy lorry on ice makes something move in the water underneath it, and it moves faster the faster the lorry goes.

title: The Sentence That Saved His Neck
situation: In 17th-century London, a thief who cannot read or write is sentenced to hang. The night before his trial ends, his cellmate makes him repeat one short sentence over and over until he knows it by heart. In court the next morning the thief speaks that sentence aloud, and instead of being hanged he is burnt on the thumb with a hot iron and released. What was going on?
solution: Under the old English law of 'benefit of clergy', a man who could prove he was a clergyman was handed over to the lenient church courts instead of being hanged, and the test of being a clergyman was simply to read a passage from the Bible. The court always used the same verse, so illiterate prisoners learnt it by heart and recited it while pretending to read, and the judges mostly let it pass. To stop a man claiming the privilege twice, his thumb was branded with a hot iron, so the scar showed any future court that he had already used up his one escape.
keyFacts: A law let anyone who could read (as proof of being a cleric) escape hanging
The court always used the same Bible verse, so he memorised it and pretended to read it
The thumb brand marked him so he could never use the privilege again
hints: The sentence was not a confession, a plea, or a lie about the crime.
The court was testing whether he had a certain skill, and he only had to appear to have it.
Which people in those days were expected to be able to read, and what book would they read from?

title: Bedtime Story in the Blackout
situation: Every night Matthew reads a bedtime story to his son. One night the power goes out and the house is plunged into darkness. Yet Matthew keeps reading and finishes the story. How can he read in the dark?
solution: Matthew is blind. He always reads bedtime stories to his son from a braille book, feeling the words with his fingers. So the blackout made no difference to him, and he finished the story as usual.
keyFacts: Matthew is blind
He reads from a braille book by touch, so he doesn't need light
hints: Think about how Matthew normally reads, not just on this night.
Matthew doesn't use his eyes to read at all.
The book he reads from has raised dots.

title: The Cold That Killed
situation: Anthony caught an ordinary cold. He could never have imagined that this cold would be the cause of his death. How did a simple cold kill him?
solution: There was a gas leak in Anthony's house, but because he had a cold he could not smell the gas. When he lit a fire to cook his dinner, the gas ignited and he died.
keyFacts: There was a gas leak in his house
His cold meant he couldn't smell the gas
He lit a fire to cook, which set off the gas
hints: The cold didn't make him seriously ill.
The cold took away one of his senses.
He couldn't smell something dangerous in his kitchen before he started cooking.

title: The Wrong Man Arrested
situation: A car driver makes an unexpected turn at a crossroads and crashes into a bike. When the police arrive, they arrest a different man, and the person who was driving is taken home. Why?
solution: The driver was a learner having a driving lesson. The instructor told him to make the wrong turn at the crossroads, which caused the crash. The police held the driving instructor responsible, so they arrested him and took the learner home.
keyFacts: The driver was a learner on a driving lesson
The instructor told him to make the turn
The police held the instructor responsible
hints: The man who was arrested was in the car.
The driver was not yet fully qualified to drive.
The man arrested was the one giving the instructions.

title: The Bandit's Bedroom
situation: Venezuelan police tried several times to arrest a well-known bandit. They knew where he lived, and they came to his house with an arrest warrant. But each time they entered, he locked himself in his bedroom, and the police had no choice but to leave empty-handed. Why couldn't they arrest him?
solution: His house sat on the border between Venezuela and Colombia. The front door and half the house were in Venezuela, but the bedroom was in Colombia. Venezuelan police have no jurisdiction in Colombia, so they could not arrest him while he stayed in the bedroom.
keyFacts: The house straddled the Venezuela–Colombia border
The bedroom was in Colombia
Venezuelan police had no jurisdiction there
hints: The locked door itself wasn't what stopped the police.
Where exactly is his bedroom, on a map?
The bedroom is in a different country from the front door.

title: Ransom in the Call-Box
situation: A rich man's son is kidnapped, and the kidnapper demands that the father leave an expensive diamond in a phone box in a city park. The police surround the park to catch the criminal. The father does exactly as he is told, yet the police cannot stop the diamond being taken from the phone box, and they never catch the kidnapper. How did he do it?
solution: When the father reached the phone box, he found a carrier pigeon in a cage with a note attached. The note told him to put the diamond in a small pouch on the pigeon's neck and let the bird out of its cage. When he did so, the pigeon flew across the city to its home loft, and the police couldn't follow it.
keyFacts: A carrier pigeon was waiting in the phone box
The father put the diamond in a pouch on the pigeon and released it
The pigeon flew home across the city, where the police couldn't follow
hints: The kidnapper never came near the phone box.
Something alive was waiting in the phone box for the father.
The diamond left the park by air.

title: The Stop No Bus Uses
situation: Beside a pleasant road stands a bus stop that is fully kept up, complete with a timetable. Yet no bus or any other public transport ever stops there. Why was it built?
solution: The stop is in Germany, next to a nursing home for people with dementia, and a timetable of supposed bus routes hangs on it. Residents who tried to wander off would go to the bus stop, sit down and patiently wait for their bus. When staff noticed that a resident had been missing for a while, they simply went and fetched them from the stop.
keyFacts: It stands next to a nursing home for people with dementia
Residents who wander off go and wait at the stop
Staff collect them from there safely
hints: The stop is meant to be used by people, just not to catch a bus.
Think about who lives in the building next to it.
It's a safe place for confused residents who try to leave.

title: Beware of Pickpockets
situation: Signs once appeared on one of the main squares in Prague: 'Attention! Beware of pickpockets!' The local police knew that the square really was full of pickpockets, yet they kept tearing the signs down. Why?
solution: The square was always crowded with tourists, and it was the pickpockets themselves who put the signs up. People who read a warning automatically checked that their valuables were still there. The watching thieves then knew exactly where to find their targets, so the police tore the signs down to stop people unknowingly helping to rob themselves.
keyFacts: The pickpockets put the signs up themselves
Reading the sign made people check their valuables
This showed the thieves where the valuables were kept
hints: The police were not the ones who put the signs up.
What is the first thing you do after reading such a warning?
When people pat their pockets to check, they reveal where their wallets are.

title: Green Lipstick
situation: Every day, a man puts on green lipstick before work. Yet almost nobody ever notices it. Why does he wear it?
solution: In the 20th century, television was still black and white, and the cameras had red filters that absorbed red, so red lipstick couldn't be seen on the lips. TV presenters therefore wore green lipstick to make their lips look more expressive on screen.
keyFacts: He works on black-and-white television
The cameras' red filters made red lipstick invisible
Green lipstick made his lips show up on screen
hints: Plenty of people see him every day, just not in person.
This happened decades ago, before colour pictures were common.
On black-and-white TV cameras, red lips didn't show up, but green ones did.

title: The Phantom
situation: For 15 years, German police were baffled by one person who seemed to be behind thefts, killings and car crimes across the country. By 2008 they had spent 14,000 working hours and more than 15 million euros hunting this criminal, without success. How is that possible?
solution: In 2009 the police finally found the 'criminal': a 71-year-old Polish woman who had worked for many years packing cotton buds at a factory in Bavaria. Those were the cotton buds used to collect DNA samples, so her DNA turned up at every crime scene. The case became known as the Phantom of Heilbronn.
keyFacts: The link between the crimes was DNA evidence
The cotton buds used for DNA sampling were contaminated
The DNA belonged to a woman who packed the buds at the factory
hints: The police linked all these crimes through forensic evidence.
The 'criminal' never set foot at any of the crime scenes.
The DNA came from the equipment used to take the samples.

title: The Vanishing Peelers
situation: A company made knives for peeling potatoes. To boost sales, the makers reasoned that if the knives went missing more often at home, people would have to buy new ones. How did they make their peelers disappear?
solution: The company started making its potato peelers in the same colour as potato peel. The knife blended in with the peelings and was often thrown away along with them, so customers had to buy replacements.
keyFacts: The peelers were coloured like potato peel
They blended in with the peelings and were thrown away with them
hints: The company changed how the knife looked, not how it worked.
Think about what ends up in the bin after peeling potatoes.
The handle was made the same colour as the peelings.

title: Beulah and Craig
situation: Beulah died in the Appalachians, while Craig died at sea. Everyone was much happier about Craig's death. How come?
solution: Beulah and Craig were hurricanes, not people. Beulah blew itself out over land in the Appalachians, where it could do damage to where people live. Craig died out at sea, so everyone was glad it never came ashore.
keyFacts: Beulah and Craig were hurricanes (storms), not people
A storm that dies at sea never hits land, so people were relieved
hints: Beulah and Craig were never alive in the usual sense.
Weather services give names to some things every year.
Where would you rather a hurricane ended: over the mountains where people live, or far out at sea?

title: The Silent Exam
situation: Students are taking an exam at a military academy. One of them picks an exam ticket and goes to his seat to prepare. A few minutes later he walks up to the professor, silently hands over his record book and leaves the room, and he gets top marks. Why?
solution: It was an exam in Morse code. While the students were preparing, the professor kept tapping out a message in Morse saying that any student who came up to him would get top marks. The only student who understood the tapping walked up, handed over his record book and got top marks.
keyFacts: The exam was a Morse code exam
The professor was tapping a Morse message offering top marks to anyone who came up
The student understood the tapping and took up the offer
hints: What the student did was an answer to something he noticed in the room.
The professor wasn't just sitting quietly during the exam; he was making a sound.
Think about what kind of code a military academy would teach, one you can tap on a desk.

title: Half a Goal
situation: In the 1940s, a real football match in Brazil ended with the unusual score of 0.5–0. How could a team score half a goal?
solution: With the score at 0–0, a penalty kick was taken and the seam of the ball burst. The inner rubber bladder went into the goal, but the outer leather casing rolled away outside it. The referee ruled that this was half a goal, so the match ended 0.5–0.
keyFacts: The ball burst during a penalty kick
The inner bladder went into the goal while the leather casing did not
The referee counted it as half a goal
hints: Nobody made a mistake with the scoreboard: the referee really did award half a goal.
Something happened to the ball itself during a kick.
Old footballs had a rubber bladder inside a leather casing. What if the two parted ways?

title: Late for Class
situation: George was late for a maths class and misunderstood what the teacher meant. Yet his mistake brought him reward and recognition. What happened?
solution: The American mathematician George Dantzig arrived very late for a class and saw some problems written on the blackboard. He thought they were homework, spent several days working on them and eventually found the answers. It turned out they were two famous 'unsolvable' problems that many scientists had been struggling with.
keyFacts: He thought problems on the blackboard were homework
They were actually famous unsolved problems
He solved them, not knowing they were thought unsolvable
hints: Because he was late, George missed what the teacher said about something written on the board.
He treated some examples of a thing like an ordinary assignment.
The problems on the board were meant as examples of problems nobody had solved yet.

title: The Royal Trendsetter
situation: King George IV, who ruled England from 1820 to 1830, was not an outstanding ruler, but he is known as a footwear trendsetter. His shoes were fundamentally different from those of his contemporaries, and the innovation caught on so well that today everyone takes it for granted. What was it?
solution: George IV was the first to have a separate right boot and left boot. Before that, all shoes and boots were made the same for both feet. The idea caught on and is now standard.
keyFacts: His boots were made differently for the left and right foot
Before that, shoes were identical for both feet
hints: The innovation has nothing to do with colour, material or decoration.
Think about the shape of a pair of shoes.
Take your two shoes off and compare them. Would they always have looked like that?

title: On the Back of the Cheque
situation: A man finishes lunch at a restaurant and the waiter brings the bill. He writes a cheque for the full amount, then suddenly turns it over and writes a few words of congratulations to the owner on the back. Why?
solution: The man was Salvador Dalí, and this was his trick for not really paying restaurant bills. He signed a cheque for the full amount and wrote warm congratulations to the owner on the back. He counted on the owner seeing a cheque autographed by the famous artist as a collectible worth far more than the meal, so it would be kept or displayed and never cashed.
keyFacts: The diner was the famous artist Salvador Dalí
His signed and inscribed cheque was worth more as a collectible than the bill
The owner would keep it and never cash it, so Dalí ate for free
hints: The man is very famous.
The words on the back make the cheque worth more than the money written on the front.
He was an artist, and his signature was valuable. Would you cash a personal note from Salvador Dalí?

title: Seat Belts and the Hospital
situation: A city had a very high number of people injured in car accidents, so the authorities made wearing seat belts compulsory, and people obeyed. The number of crashes stayed the same, but the number of injured people turning up at hospital actually rose. Why?
solution: The seat belt law worked. Many people who would have died in crashes without a seat belt survived, but they were injured. So instead of being counted as deaths, they went to hospital, and hospital admissions went up.
keyFacts: Seat belts turned many deaths into survivable injuries
People who would have died now went to hospital injured, raising the count
hints: The seat belt law was actually a success.
Think about what used to happen to the people who were worst hurt in crashes.
If fewer people die in crashes, where do those survivors end up?

title: The Builders' Countermove
situation: Landlords used to delay paying the people who built and repaired their houses, or even threw them out without paying at all. Then the builders came up with an unusual trick that made landlords pay them in full straight away. What did they do?
solution: When laying a foundation or doing repairs, the builders hid a raw egg somewhere in the house. Over time it began to rot. If the landlord paid them, they came back and took the egg away. If he threw them out, the egg eventually stank, and it was very hard to find where it had been hidden.
keyFacts: Builders hid a raw egg in the building during the work
The egg would rot and stink, and only the builders knew where it was
They removed it only when paid in full
hints: The builders left something behind inside the house.
It was harmless at first, but time would change that.
Think of something from the kitchen that smells terrible when it goes off.

title: The Expensive Fake
situation: A woman buys a painting signed 'I. Repin' for ten roubles at an antique stall, and later shows it to the artist Ilya Repin, whom she knows personally. As soon as it is confirmed to be a fake, the painting becomes worth ten times as much. How?
solution: When the woman showed Repin the painting at a friend's gathering, he laughed and wrote at the bottom: 'This is not Repin. I. Repin.' The painting went back to the market and sold for one hundred roubles. The fake itself was worthless, but it now carried the famous artist's genuine autograph, and that is what made it valuable.
keyFacts: The famous artist Repin himself confirmed it was a fake
He wrote on it that it wasn't his work and signed it
His genuine signature made the fake valuable
hints: The person who declared it a fake is important.
The painting was changed in one small way when it was found to be a fake.
Now the fake carries something the real artist added himself.

title: How to Beat Nick Faldo
situation: A man challenged golf champion Nick Faldo to a match on one condition: he would choose the time and the place. Faldo agreed. The challenger won. How?
solution: The challenger was blind, and he chose to play the match on a moonless night. He was used to playing golf without seeing, since blind people can play golf with help from sighted people. Faldo was not used to playing in the dark, so he lost.
keyFacts: The challenger was blind
He chose to play at night in total darkness
Darkness made no difference to him but put Faldo at a disadvantage
hints: The choice of time mattered more than the choice of course.
Think about conditions that would bother a champion but not his opponent.
What if the challenger couldn't see anyway?

title: The Mayor's Greeting
situation: A priest who is leaving town gives a farewell speech. The mayor turns up near the end of it to say a few words of greeting, but he is shot dead before he can finish. Why was the mayor killed?
solution: In his speech the priest recalled his first day in the town and said that the very first confession he ever heard there was a murderer's. The mayor had missed that part. When he arrived, he proudly said that he had been the priest's first confessor, and so without knowing it he confessed to the murder. The victim's brother was in the crowd and shot him.
keyFacts: The priest said his first confession in the town came from a murderer
The mayor arrived late and did not hear that part
The mayor boasted that he was the priest's first confessor, giving himself away
The murder victim's brother shot him
hints: What the priest said before the mayor arrived matters a great deal.
The priest talked about his first day in the town and the first confession he ever heard there.
The mayor proudly announced he had been the priest's very first confessor, and someone in the crowd had a personal reason to act on that.

title: Death in the Sauna
situation: A man is found dead on the floor of a sauna. Next to him is a thermos flask. There is no weapon anywhere. How did he die?
solution: He was murdered. The killer brought a weapon made of ice, an ice screwdriver, in the thermos flask to keep it frozen, and stabbed him with it. In the heat of the sauna the ice melted, so no weapon was left behind.
keyFacts: He was murdered, stabbed
The weapon was made of ice
The thermos kept the ice weapon frozen
The sauna's heat melted the weapon away
hints: Think about why someone would need a thermos in a sauna.
The weapon is still in the room, just not in its original form.
The murder weapon was made of ice, and the sauna's heat made it disappear.

title: One Step Back
situation: A man takes one step backwards and dies. He was simply doing his job. What happened?
solution: He was a window cleaner working high up on a building. When he finished cleaning a window, he stepped back to check that it was completely clean. That step took him over the edge, and he fell to his death.
keyFacts: He was a window cleaner
He was working high up on a building
He stepped back to admire his work and fell
hints: His job was done high above the ground.
He wanted to get a better look at the job he had just finished.
He was a window cleaner who stepped back to check the glass and fell off the building.

title: The Healed Finger
situation: A man cuts his finger. He puts it in some water, and when he pulls his hand out, the wound has gone. How?
solution: The water was a river full of piranhas. The blood attracted them and they ate his finger, so the wound was gone along with it.
keyFacts: The water was a river full of piranhas
The piranhas ate the injured finger
The wound disappeared because the finger did
hints: The wound did not heal.
Something living in the water was drawn to the blood.
The river was full of piranhas, and they ate the whole finger.

title: The 500-Euro Porsche
situation: A woman sells her husband's Porsche for only 500 euros. There is nothing mechanically wrong with the car. Why is she selling it so cheaply?
solution: Her husband killed himself inside the car, and his body was not found for several days. The smell of the body got into the car and never went away. Nobody would pay a normal price for it, so she had to sell it for next to nothing.
keyFacts: The husband died inside the car
His body was only found days later
The smell of death stayed in the car, making it nearly worthless
hints: The husband is no longer around.
Something happened inside the car that left a permanent trace.
He killed himself in the car, and the smell of his body never came out.

title: The Unbeaten Ford Record
situation: In 1930, two men drove a Ford from New York to Los Angeles, about 5,375 km, in 18 days. They used ordinary roads and an ordinary car, yet they set a world record that has never been beaten. How?
solution: They drove the whole way in reverse. Crossing the country backwards set a record for reverse driving over that distance, and nobody has ever beaten it.
keyFacts: They drove the entire way in reverse
The record is for backwards driving, not for speed
hints: The record is not about speed.
It is about how they drove the car, not the car itself.
They did the whole trip in reverse gear.

title: The Sunken Car
situation: A man driving fast spins off the road and crashes into a river. His arm is broken, he cannot undo his seatbelt, and the car sinks to the bottom of the river. Two hours later, rescuers find him still alive. How did he survive?
solution: The river was shallow. Even with the car sitting on the riverbed, the water only came up to the man's chest, so he could keep breathing until help arrived.
keyFacts: The river was shallow
The water only reached his chest while he sat in the car
He could breathe the whole time
hints: Do not picture a deep river.
Think about how high the water rose inside the car.
The car hit the bottom, but the water only came up to his chest.

title: The Wrong-Way Truck Driver
situation: A police officer sees a truck driver clearly going the wrong way down a one-way street. The officer does not try to stop him. Why not?
solution: The truck driver was walking, not driving his truck. A person on foot can go either way down a one-way street, so he was breaking no rule.
keyFacts: The truck driver was on foot
No law was broken
hints: Nobody said he was in his truck.
Being a truck driver is his job, not what he was doing at that moment.
He was walking down the street.

title: Weight Loss Miracle
situation: A woman walks into a small room and presses a button. Within a few seconds she has lost twenty pounds. She has not exercised, dieted or had surgery. How did she lose the weight so quickly?
solution: The room is an elevator. She pressed the button for a lower floor, and as the elevator accelerated downwards her apparent weight dropped. The scale reading, not her body, changed: gravitational acceleration temporarily reduced her measured weight by about twenty pounds.
keyFacts: The room is an elevator
The elevator is accelerating downwards
Only her apparent weight on a scale changes, not her actual mass
hints: The room she walked into is not a normal room — it moves.
Think about what a bathroom scale reads while you are going down quickly.
She is in a descending elevator; downward acceleration makes her weigh less for a moment.

title: Two Words, Sixty Sheets
situation: Every two weeks, a woman writes the same two words on sixty separate sheets of paper. She is not practising her handwriting and she is not copying anything out. Why does she do it?
solution: The woman owns a business with sixty employees. The two words are her first and last name, and she is signing the paychecks. Payroll runs every two weeks, so the same ritual repeats each pay period.
keyFacts: The two words are her own name — a signature
She is signing paychecks
She owns a business with sixty employees, paid biweekly
hints: The two words are always exactly the same, and they are hers.
The sheets of paper are worth money to the people who receive them.
She is the boss signing sixty paychecks on payday.

title: The Boat Ladder
situation: A ten-foot ladder hangs over the side of a boat, and three feet of it are under the water. The tide then rises by five feet. How much of the ladder is underwater now?
solution: Still three feet. The boat floats, so it rises with the tide and the ladder rises with the boat. The amount of ladder below the waterline does not change no matter how high the tide comes.
keyFacts: Still three feet of ladder underwater
The boat floats and rises with the tide
The ladder rises along with the boat
hints: The ladder is attached to something that is not fixed to the seabed.
Ask yourself what the boat does as the water level goes up.
The boat floats up with the tide, so nothing changes: three feet.

title: Eight Slices, Three Cuts
situation: It is your birthday and you have invited eight friends. You must divide your birthday cake into eight equal-sized pieces, but you are allowed only three cuts of the knife. How do you do it?
solution: Make two vertical cuts across the top of the cake, crossing at the centre, to produce four equal pieces. Then make the third cut horizontally, straight through the middle of the cake's height, slicing every piece into a top half and a bottom half. That gives eight equal pieces from three cuts.
keyFacts: Two vertical cuts crossing at the centre give four pieces
The third cut is horizontal, through the cake's height
Each of the four pieces is halved into a top and a bottom, making eight
hints: Two cuts from above already give you four pieces — you only have one cut left.
The cake is a three-dimensional object, not a flat circle.
Cut it sideways through the middle so every piece becomes a top and a bottom.

title: The Commotion
situation: Several voices can be heard coming from a room, and there is the sound of a commotion going on. When someone opens the door to see what is happening, there is only one person there, sitting quietly. That person is perfectly sane. Where did the voices come from?
solution: The voices came from a television set that the person was watching. The commotion was part of the programme, not something happening in the room. The single quiet occupant was simply the viewer.
keyFacts: The voices came from a television
The person in the room was watching it
No one else was ever in the room
hints: The person in the room is not talking to themselves.
The other voices belong to people who were never in the house.
A television was playing.

title: A Quick Choke
situation: A man is sitting alone in a dark room when he suddenly stops breathing and cannot speak or call out. A few seconds later he is breathing normally again, and there is no sign of what blocked his airway. What happened?
solution: He was watching a film in the dark and choked on an ice cube from his drink. The ice lodged in his throat and stopped him breathing, but it melted within seconds and the airway cleared. That is why nothing was left behind to show what had choked him.
keyFacts: He choked on an ice cube from his drink
The ice melted in his throat within seconds
The room was dark because he was watching a movie
hints: Something was blocking his throat, but it did not stay there.
Whatever it was disappeared on its own, which is why there is no evidence.
It was an ice cube, and it melted.

title: Born in 1957, Died in 1956
situation: John was born in 1957 and died in 1956, and he was 82 years old when he died. None of this is a mistake and no time travel is involved. How is it possible?
solution: 1957 and 1956 are not years but room numbers in a hospital. John was born in room 1957 and, 82 years later, died in room 1956 of the same hospital. The numbers only look like dates.
keyFacts: 1957 and 1956 are room numbers, not years
He was born in room 1957 and died in room 1956
He was 82 when he died, so the numbers cannot be dates
hints: The numbers are not dates at all.
Both numbers refer to the same kind of place — and he was in that place at both ends of his life.
They are hospital room numbers.

title: One Match in a Dark Room
situation: A man is stuck in a dark room. He has exactly one match, and in the room there is a fireplace, a candle and an oil lamp. What should he light first?
solution: He should light the match first. It is impossible to light the oil lamp, the fireplace or the candle without first striking and lighting the match itself. The trick is that the question assumes the answer must be one of the three objects in the room.
keyFacts: He lights the match itself first
Nothing else in the room can be lit until the match is burning
The listed objects (fireplace, candle, oil lamp) are a distraction
hints: Don't worry about which object burns longest or is most useful — think about the order of events.
Before anything in the room can catch fire, something else has to be burning already.
The answer is the thing in his hand, not the things around him.

title: The Chicken Gun
situation: In the 1950s, American engineers invented a device they called a chicken gun: a large-diameter cannon powered by compressed air, loaded with dead chickens. It was built entirely seriously, and it is still used today. What was it for?
solution: The chicken gun is a compressed-air cannon used to fire dead chickens at aircraft components. It simulates high-speed bird strikes of the kind a plane suffers in flight. Engineers use it to test how much damage jet engines, windshields and other parts take in a collision with a bird.
keyFacts: It fires the birds at aircraft parts
It simulates a bird strike at flight speed
It is a safety/durability test for engines and windshields
hints: Nobody eats these chickens — they are ammunition, not food.
The target is a machine, and the point is to see how badly it breaks.
Think about what birds do to a plane taking off at high speed.

title: The Pear in the Bottle
situation: In a shop you find a bottle of brandy with a full-grown pear floating inside it. The pear is far too big to pass through the neck, the bottle has not been cut or repaired, and the glass is in one piece. How did the pear get in there?
solution: The pear is never put into the bottle at all — it grows inside it. While the fruit is still tiny, the bottle is tied over it on the tree branch, and the pear then grows to full size within the glass. Afterwards the bottle is taken off the tree and filled with brandy.
keyFacts: The pear was never pushed through the neck
The bottle was attached to the branch while the fruit was still small
The pear grew to full size inside the bottle
hints: The bottle did not come to the pear — it went to the pear.
Think about when the pear was small enough to fit through the neck.
The bottle spent part of the summer hanging on a tree.

title: Splish, Splash!
situation: Tim is out sailing his boat when his watch slips off his wrist and falls overboard. He is an excellent diver and the water is clear and calm, yet he cannot get the watch back. Why not?
solution: Tim was sailing on the Dead Sea. The water there is so dense with salt that a swimmer is pushed back to the surface. However hard he tried, he could not dive deep enough to reach the watch.
keyFacts: He was on the Dead Sea
The very high salt concentration makes the water extremely buoyant
He physically could not dive down deep enough
hints: It has nothing to do with his diving skill or the depth of the water.
The problem is the water itself, not the watch.
In this particular sea, people famously float without trying.

title: Savages Can Be Clever Too
situation: Aborigines lived on an island in the middle of the ocean. On the sea bed near them lay porcelain vases from a shipwreck, and for a hundred years even the most experienced divers had failed to bring them up. Yet the islanders found a way to recover the porcelain and grow rich. How did they do it?
solution: They used octopuses. They caught octopuses, tied them to ropes and lowered them into the water, then waited until the animals found hiding places inside the porcelain bowls and vessels among the wreckage. Octopuses are stubborn creatures and refused to let go of their new home even when hauled up by the rope, so the porcelain came up with them. Sometimes an octopus brought up a stone instead, but the method worked well enough.
keyFacts: They did not dive for the porcelain themselves
They used tethered octopuses lowered on ropes
Octopuses hid inside the vases and would not let go when pulled up
hints: They let something else do the diving for them.
The helper was a sea animal that likes to squeeze into hollow spaces.
When you pull it up by the rope, it clings to its new shelter — and the shelter is a vase.

title: John's Favourite Place
situation: In 18th-century Stockholm, John loved going to a certain place and had many reasons for doing so. His wife Mary hated it, and so did the other women of the city — not only because of what went on there, but because they simply could not get to it. Why?
solution: The place was a drinking house reached by a street no more than a metre wide. Drunkards loved it because they could hold on to the walls on both sides as they staggered along. Their wives, however, could not follow them down it: the hooped dresses of the period got stuck between the walls.
keyFacts: It was a tavern at the end of an extremely narrow street
Drunk men could steady themselves on both walls
Women's wide hooped dresses would not fit through
hints: The obstacle is the street, not the door.
The street is barely a metre wide — an advantage for a drunk man.
Think about what women wore in the 18th century and how wide it was.

title: Running to Meet the Train
situation: A man was walking along a railway line when he saw a train coming straight towards him. Instead of turning and running away, he ran as fast as he could towards the oncoming train. He survived. Why did he run at it?
solution: The man was inside a tunnel. He was nearer to the end the train was coming from than to the far end, so running towards the train was the only way to get out of the tunnel before it reached him. As soon as he was clear of the tunnel mouth he jumped off the track to safety.
keyFacts: He was inside a railway tunnel with no room to stand aside
The near exit was the one the train was approaching from
He got out of the tunnel mouth and jumped clear of the track
hints: There was nowhere to step aside where he was standing.
He was not trying to reach the train — he was trying to reach something behind it.
Picture a tunnel: which end was closer to him?

title: The Silk Scarf
situation: Bill always wore a silk scarf to work, in every kind of weather. It was not for warmth and it was not for fashion — without it he could not have done his job properly. What was his job, and why did he need the scarf?
solution: Bill was a First World War pilot. Early military aircraft had open cockpits and flew at up to 150 km/h, so pilots wore thick leather clothing against the wind. With no long-range detection systems, a pilot had to keep turning his head to scan for enemy planes — at least every twenty seconds — and some rubbed their necks raw, even bloody, against the stiff collar. A white silk scarf, being smooth yet dense, protected against the headwind and acted as a smooth layer between skin and collar.
keyFacts: He was a WWI pilot in an open cockpit
He had to keep turning his head constantly to spot enemy aircraft
The stiff leather collar chafed his neck, and smooth silk prevented it
hints: The scarf protects a part of his body that moves a great deal at work.
His job involves constantly looking around in a strong wind.
Open cockpit, heavy leather collar, and a neck that has to swivel every twenty seconds.

title: The Cunning Artist
situation: An artist accepted a commission to paint a very ugly and arrogant woman. Everybody warned him she would never pay a penny for the finished portrait, and indeed she refused it. Two days later she came back and begged him to sell it to her. Why?
solution: The artist had sent the portrait to an exhibition under the title 'The Penny Pincher'. The picture set the whole town gossiping about her, and to get it taken down she had to come back to the artist and buy it.
keyFacts: He put the portrait on public display in an exhibition
He gave it a title mocking her refusal to pay
The gossip forced her to buy it to have it removed
hints: The artist did not destroy the painting — he found it an audience.
What he added to the picture was not paint but words.
The title told everyone exactly why she had not paid.

title: Marmalade at School
situation: Bill managed to skip school again and again without ever being marked absent, and marmalade was what made it possible. He was not bribing anyone with sweets. How did marmalade help him?
solution: From 2010, Australian schools used fingerprint scanners to check attendance. Bill discovered that the gelatin in marmalade bears could fool the scanner: he pressed his finger into a gummy bear to take an impression of his fingerprint, then had a classmate hold the sweet against the scanner for him. The system recognised the fingerprint and recorded Bill as present in class.
keyFacts: The school checked attendance with fingerprint scanners
Gelatin from a marmalade bear took an impression of his fingerprint
A classmate presented the sweet to the scanner so Bill was marked present
hints: The marmalade was not eaten — it was used as a tool.
The school registered attendance with a machine, not a teacher's roll call.
Gelatin holds the shape of whatever you press into it, including a fingertip.

title: (Un)luck
situation: Because of a mistake Nils made at work, his upstairs neighbour Martha was unable to wash her dishes. Martha's husband, however, was delighted — and Nils was fired. What happened?
solution: Nils was a bartender in the café on the ground floor and mixed up the pipes when connecting the taps. When Martha turned on her water tap upstairs, beer came out of it, so she could not wash up — while down in the bar, water splashed out of the beer tap. Martha's husband was very pleased with the arrangement, but the bartender lost his job.
keyFacts: Nils was a bartender downstairs and connected the taps the wrong way round
Beer came out of Martha's water tap
Water came out of the bar's beer tap, and Nils was fired for it
hints: Something did come out of Martha's tap — just not water.
Her husband's delight is the clue to what it was.
Think about what business is on the ground floor and what pipes run through the building.
